children.note: How living soil works, how to judge it, and how plants show what they lack.
Soil is alive: billions of organisms in every handful feed on plant carbon and on each other, recycling nutrients and building structure. Understanding this web is the basis of biological farming.
How to tell whether a soil is healthy, from simple spade and water tests in the field to laboratory analysis. Includes how to sample correctly and read a soil report.

Plants show nutrient shortages through colour, shape and where on the plant the damage starts. Learning to read these signs, then confirming with a soil or leaf test, lets you choose the right compost, mineral or microbe instead of guessing.
Microbes that turn air nitrogen into plant food.

Rhizobia are bacteria that form pink nodules on legume roots and fix air nitrogen for the plant. Using the right strain for each crop group, applied carefully on seed, can supply much of a legume's nitrogen.

Azotobacter is a free-living, aerobic soil bacterium that fixes nitrogen and releases growth hormones near roots of non-legume crops. It works best in soils rich in organic matter and complements, not replaces, good fertility.

Nitrogen-fixing helpers for non-legume crops: Azospirillum on cereal roots, Gluconacetobacter inside sugarcane, and cyanobacteria and Azolla in rice fields. They supply part of the crop's nitrogen and improve rooting.
Microbes that unlock phosphorus, potash, zinc and sulphur, and fungi that extend roots.

Soil bacteria and fungi that release phosphorus locked up as calcium, iron or aluminium phosphates. Used with compost and rock phosphate, they help crops get more from the phosphorus already in the soil.
Soil bacteria that unlock potassium, zinc, sulphur, silicon and iron already present in soil or minerals. They complement fertilisers and work best with organic matter and moisture.

Soil fungi that partner with plant roots, extending them with fine hyphae to bring in phosphorus, zinc and water in exchange for plant sugars. Most crops benefit; protecting native fungi matters as much as adding inoculum.
Beneficial fungi, bacteria, viruses and nematodes that suppress diseases and pests.

Trichoderma is a group of soil fungi used as a biological fungicide. It attacks and crowds out root-rotting fungi and also helps roots grow, so it is mainly used to prevent soil-borne diseases rather than cure them.
Three groups of beneficial bacteria used as biological disease control agents. They protect plants by producing antibiotics, competing for iron and space, and switching on the plant's own defences.

Living fungi, bacteria, viruses and nematodes that make insect pests and nematodes sick. They act more slowly and more selectively than chemical pesticides and work best as part of integrated pest management (IPM).
Turning waste into soil food, on the farm.
Compost is organic waste turned by microbes (and worms) into a stable, humus-rich material that feeds soil life. Making it well means managing food, air, water and temperature for the decomposers.

Liquids and solids that farmers ferment on the farm from dung, urine, plants, fish or forest soil to feed soil life and protect crops. They are cheap and local, but much of their reputation rests on field experience rather than controlled trials.
Putting it together on the farm and in the business.

Farming that aims to rebuild soil health, water cycling and biodiversity while staying productive. It is defined more by principles and outcomes than by a fixed rulebook, and practices must fit the local context.
Biofertilizers and biopesticides are living products. They only work if they arrive alive, are applied the right way, and are used as part of a wider soil and crop plan.

nodeData.note: Soil is alive: billions of organisms in every handful feed on plant carbon and on each other, recycling nutrients and building structure. Understanding this web is the basis of biological farming.

children.topic: What the soil food web is
children.note: The soil food web is the community of organisms living in soil and the feeding links between them. Energy enters through plants and dead organic matter and passes from microbes to the animals that eat them.
Green plants capture sunlight and push carbon into the soil as roots, root exudates and dead leaves. Almost all soil life depends on this carbon, directly or indirectly.

manas.q: Where does almost all the energy in the soil food web come from?

children.note: Primary decomposers (bacteria, fungi) feed on organic matter and exudates. Grazers such as protozoa, nematodes and micro-arthropods eat them, and predators eat the grazers.
This web recycles nutrients, builds soil structure, suppresses some diseases and breaks down residues. A biological product works only if it can find food and a home in this web.
Soil holds a huge diversity of life, from microscopic bacteria to earthworms and insects. Each group does a different job in the system.
Tiny single-celled organisms and the most numerous group in soil. They decompose simple compounds, cycle nutrients, and some fix nitrogen or solubilise phosphorus.
A gram of fertile soil usually holds hundreds of millions to around a billion bacterial cells. Most of them have never been grown in a laboratory.

manas.q: Roughly how many bacteria live in one gram of fertile soil?

links.label: 📄 Source: FAO – State of knowledge of soil biodiversity (2020)

children.note: Examples include nitrogen fixers (Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azospirillum), nitrifiers (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter), phosphate solubilisers (Bacillus, Pseudomonas) and decomposers.
Bacteria produce sticky sugars (polysaccharides) that bind fine particles into micro-aggregates. This helps create pore space for air and water.
Fungi grow as long thread-like hyphae that can bridge gaps between soil particles. They break down tough material such as lignin and cellulose in straw and wood.
Saprophytic fungi digest dead plant material, especially woody and fibrous residues that bacteria handle poorly. They are important in making stable organic matter.
Mycorrhizal fungi live in partnership with roots: the plant feeds them sugars and the fungi extend the root system to fetch phosphorus, zinc and water. Most crops form arbuscular mycorrhiza (AMF).

manas.q: What do arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi give the plant in exchange for sugars?

children.note: Some fungi such as Trichoderma attack disease fungi, while others like Fusarium, Pythium and Rhizoctonia cause root diseases. A diverse community helps keep pathogens in check.
Fungal networks are easily broken by ploughing and harmed by some fungicides. Soils under frequent tillage tend to become more bacteria-dominated.
Actinomycetes are filament-forming bacteria, such as Streptomyces, that look a little like fungi. They decompose tough materials and work well in drier, neutral to alkaline soils.
The pleasant smell of freshly dug or wet soil comes largely from geosmin, a compound made by Streptomyces. A sweet earthy smell is a good sign of active biology.

manas.q: Which organisms produce geosmin, the 'earthy' smell of healthy soil?

children.note: Many antibiotics used in medicine, such as streptomycin, were first found in soil Streptomyces. In soil these compounds help them compete and can suppress some pathogens.
Protozoa are single-celled animals (flagellates, amoebae and ciliates) that mainly eat bacteria. They are most active in the moist zone around roots.
Bacteria hold more nitrogen than protozoa need, so when protozoa eat bacteria they release the extra nitrogen as ammonium near the root. This is often called the microbial loop.

manas.q: Why does protozoa grazing on bacteria release plant-available nitrogen?

children.note: Healthy soils commonly contain thousands to tens of thousands of protozoa per gram. Their numbers rise quickly when bacteria multiply.

links.label: 📄 Source: FAO – State of knowledge of soil biodiversity (2020)

children.note: Nematodes are tiny unsegmented worms. Most are beneficial, feeding on bacteria, fungi or other nematodes; a minority are plant parasites.
Bacterial-feeders, fungal-feeders, predators and omnivores recycle nutrients and regulate other populations. Plant-parasitic types such as root-knot nematode (Meloidogyne) damage roots.

manas.q: Are most soil nematodes plant pests?

children.note: A balanced nematode community with many predators and omnivores suggests a stable, undisturbed soil. Dominance by plant parasites signals a problem.
Arthropods include mites, springtails, beetles, ants, termites and millipedes. They shred residues, mix soil and eat other organisms.
Millipedes, woodlice and some mites chew leaves and straw into small pieces. This greatly increases the surface area that microbes can attack.
In East African and Indian drylands, termites and ants are major soil engineers. They move soil, build channels and break down tough dry residues.
Earthworms swallow soil and organic matter and leave behind casts rich in available nutrients. Their burrows improve drainage, aeration and root growth.

Litter-dwellers live in surface litter, topsoil-dwellers burrow horizontally, and deep-burrowers make vertical channels. Compost worms like Eisenia fetida are litter-dwellers and do not survive well in field soil.
Casts are richer in available nutrients and microbes than surrounding soil and form stable aggregates. They are a visible sign of a working soil.

manas.q: Why are earthworm casts valuable to plants?

children.note: The rhizosphere is the thin layer of soil, a few millimetres thick, directly influenced by living roots. It is the busiest part of the soil food web.
Roots leak and actively release sugars, amino acids, organic acids, mucilage and signalling compounds. A meaningful share of the carbon a plant fixes ends up in the soil this way.

manas.q: Name three kinds of compounds found in root exudates.

children.note: In return for exudates, rhizosphere microbes release nutrients, make growth hormones and help defend roots. Plants partly shape which microbes gather around them.
Microbial numbers near roots are many times higher than in bulk soil away from roots. This is why biofertilizers are applied to seed or roots, where food is available.
Cover crops, intercrops and perennial plants keep feeding the rhizosphere between main crops. Long bare fallows starve soil life.
Soil organic matter is everything in soil that was once alive, from fresh residues to highly decomposed material. Though often only a few percent of soil weight, it drives fertility.
SOM includes living organisms, fresh residues, partly decomposed material and stable organic matter. It holds nutrients and water and feeds soil life.
Labs usually measure soil organic carbon (SOC). Organic matter is roughly 58% carbon, so SOM is commonly estimated as SOC × 1.72.

manas.q: How is soil organic matter usually estimated from organic carbon?

children.note: The active pool (fresh residues, microbial biomass) turns over in months to a few years and supplies nutrients. The stable pool persists for decades and builds structure and holding capacity.
Organic matter increases water-holding capacity, nutrient-holding (CEC), buffering against pH change and aggregate stability. In sandy and tropical soils it is often the main source of CEC.
Humus is the dark, well-decomposed part of organic matter that resists further breakdown. It gives soil its dark colour and holds nutrients and water.

Scientists now see stable organic matter mainly as microbial residues and plant compounds protected inside aggregates or bound to clay, rather than special giant 'humic' molecules. Protection, not chemistry alone, keeps carbon in soil.
Glomalin is a sticky glycoprotein linked to arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. It coats hyphae and helps glue soil particles into stable aggregates.

manas.q: Which group of fungi is associated with glomalin, and what does it do?

children.note: Add compost, manure and crop residues; keep living roots; reduce tillage; and avoid burning. Gains are slow and are usually measured over years, not one season.
Soil organisms turn nutrients locked in residues and minerals into forms plants can take up. They also store nutrients in their own bodies, reducing losses.
Nitrogen moves between air, organic matter, microbes and plants. Most soil nitrogen is held in organic forms that microbes must release.
Some bacteria convert air nitrogen (N2) into ammonia. Rhizobium does this in legume root nodules, while Azotobacter and Azospirillum do it in the root zone or soil.

manas.q: What is biological nitrogen fixation?

children.note: Microbes break down organic nitrogen in residues and manure to ammonium. Grazing by protozoa and nematodes speeds this up.
Bacteria such as Nitrosomonas convert ammonium to nitrite and Nitrobacter converts nitrite to nitrate. Nitrate is easily taken up but also easily leached.

manas.q: Which bacteria carry out the two steps of nitrification?

children.note: In waterlogged, low-oxygen soil, bacteria turn nitrate into nitrous oxide and N2 gas that escape to air. Nitrate can also leach below the roots after heavy rain.
When residues with lots of carbon and little nitrogen (like straw) are added, microbes take up soil nitrogen and crops may turn yellow for a while. A C:N below about 25:1 usually avoids this.
Phosphorus does not cycle through the air and is easily locked up by calcium in alkaline soils or iron and aluminium in acid soils. Biology helps release it.
Phosphate-solubilising bacteria and fungi release organic acids that free phosphate bound to calcium, iron or aluminium.
Microbes and roots release phosphatase enzymes that free phosphate from organic matter.
Mycorrhizal hyphae reach far beyond the root's depletion zone and bring phosphorus back to the plant. This matters most in low-P soils.
Plants take carbon dioxide from the air and pass it to soil through roots and residues. Microbes respire most of it back, while a part is stored as stable organic matter.
Soil respiration (CO2 release) is a measure of how active soil life is. Moderate, steady respiration with ongoing residue inputs is healthy.
Carbon stays longest when it is held inside aggregates or bound to clay particles. Practices that build aggregates help soils store more carbon.
Microbes also help release potassium, sulphur, zinc and iron. Some make siderophores, molecules that grab iron and make it available to roots or keep it from pathogens.
Soil structure is the way sand, silt, clay and organic matter clump together into aggregates with pores between them. Good structure lets water in and roots and air through.
Bacterial glues bind clay into micro-aggregates; fungal hyphae, roots and glomalin bind these into larger macro-aggregates. Earthworms and termites also build aggregates.

manas.q: Name three biological 'glues' or binders that build soil aggregates.

children.note: Large pores drain water and let air in; small pores store water for plants. A crumbly structure with both sizes supports roots and soil life.
Healthy soil breaks into rounded crumbs, has many root channels and worm holes, and holds together in water. Poor soil forms hard clods, crusts or dense layers.
Many common practices damage the soil food web. Knowing the causes helps farmers protect the organisms that biological inputs depend on.
Repeated ploughing breaks fungal networks and aggregates, exposes organic matter to rapid breakdown and leaves soil bare. Organic matter and earthworm numbers usually decline.

manas.q: Give two ways frequent ploughing harms soil life.

children.note: Broad-spectrum fungicides, fumigants and some soil insecticides kill beneficial organisms as well as targets. Heavy use of ammonium-based fertilisers can acidify soil over time.
Burning straw and stubble destroys organic matter and nitrogen, heats the topsoil and kills organisms near the surface. It also pollutes the air, as seen with paddy straw burning in north India.
Uncovered soil is baked by the sun, crusted by rain and washed away. The topsoil lost carries most of the organic matter and life.
Heavy machinery and grazing on wet soil squash pores and starve organisms of air. Waterlogged soils lose nitrogen and favour root-rot organisms.
Growing the same crop repeatedly narrows the food supply for soil life and lets pests and diseases build up. Rotations and mixtures support a more diverse web.
Practices that keep the soil covered, keep living roots, add diverse organic inputs and reduce disturbance help rebuild soil life.
Minimise disturbance, keep the soil covered, keep living roots as long as possible, increase plant diversity and integrate animals or manure. These are the common principles of soil health.
Well-made compost adds organic matter and a wide range of microbes. It is also an ideal carrier to multiply biofertilizers before field application.
Biofertilizers add useful organisms but they complement, rather than fully replace, nutrients from manures or fertilisers. They establish best in soils with organic matter and moisture.

nodeData.note: How to tell whether a soil is healthy, from simple spade and water tests in the field to laboratory analysis. Includes how to sample correctly and read a soil report.

children.note: A healthy soil works as a living system: it takes in water, feeds crops, supports diverse life and resists erosion. A degraded soil has lost structure, organic matter and life.
Dark, crumbly topsoil, plenty of earthworms, deep roots, quick water entry, an earthy smell and residues that break down within a season.
Even crop growth, deep roots with fine root hairs and fewer stress symptoms in dry spells point to good soil. Legume roots with pink nodules show active nitrogen fixation.

manas.q: What colour are active nitrogen-fixing nodules inside?

children.note: Crusting after rain, puddles and run-off, hard plough pans, pale colour, few worms, sour smell and residues that stay undecomposed.

Yellowing of older leaves suggests nitrogen shortage; purple tinge can mean phosphorus shortage; scorched leaf edges can mean potassium shortage; stripes on young leaves often mean zinc or iron problems. Confirm with tests before acting.
White crusts on the surface point to salts, while black slick crusts and very slow drainage suggest sodicity. These are common in irrigated drylands of India and parts of Kenya.
Soil health is assessed through physical (structure, water entry), chemical (pH, nutrients, salts) and biological (organic matter, life, respiration) indicators. Good assessment combines all three.

manas.q: What are the three groups of soil health indicators?

children.note: Many soil health checks need only a spade, a can, water and a notebook. Repeat them in the same place and season each year to see trends.
Dig a block of soil about a spade deep and examine it. Look at structure, colour, roots, smell, worms and any hard layers.
Good soil crumbles into rounded aggregates, roots grow straight down and there are worm channels. Flat plates, sideways-turning roots or a sudden hard layer signal compaction.

manas.q: What does a root that turns sideways in a spade test usually indicate?

children.note: Dig in a field and in an undisturbed spot such as a fence line or forest edge. The difference shows how much management has changed the soil.
Gently place dry soil clods in water and watch. Stable, biologically active soil stays together, while weak soil quickly falls apart and clouds the water.
Aggregates held together by roots, fungal hyphae, glomalin and microbial glues resist breaking apart in water. Tilled, low-organic-matter soil lacks these binders.

manas.q: In a slake test, what does a clod that falls apart quickly tell you?

children.note: Push a metal ring or open-ended can into the soil, pour in a fixed volume of water and time how long it takes to soak in. Slow infiltration means more run-off and erosion.
Insert the ring a few centimetres deep, line it with plastic, add the water, then pull away the plastic and start timing. Do a second run as the soil is then near field moisture.
Compare times between fields, between tilled and untilled patches, or over years. A falling time over seasons shows improving structure.
Dig a spade-sized block of topsoil when soil is moist and count earthworms. Seasonal timing matters, as worms move deep in dry or hot periods.
Ten or more worms in a spadeful is a commonly used sign of good biological health. Very few or none suggests low organic matter, disturbance or chemical harm.

manas.q: Roughly how many earthworms per spadeful is commonly taken as a good sign?

children.note: Healthy soil smells sweet and earthy because of geosmin from actinomycetes. A sour or rotten-egg smell suggests waterlogging and lack of oxygen.
Dark topsoil usually means more organic matter. Grey or blue-grey patches and mottles show poor drainage, while pale topsoil suggests low organic matter or erosion.

manas.q: What do grey or blue-grey mottles in soil indicate?

children.note: Bury a piece of cotton cloth or check last season's residues. Fast breakdown shows active microbes; residues that remain intact suggest weak biology.
Shake soil with water in a jar and let it settle; sand settles in a minute, silt in hours and clay over a day. The layers give a rough idea of soil texture.
A soil lab measures what cannot be seen in the field. Basic tests guide fertiliser and lime use; biological tests show how alive the soil is.
pH measures how acidic or alkaline soil is, on a scale of 0–14. Most crops grow best around pH 6.0–7.5.
pH controls nutrient availability: phosphorus is locked up in very acid and very alkaline soils, and aluminium becomes toxic below about pH 5.5. Many beneficial bacteria prefer near-neutral soil.

manas.q: What pH range suits most crops?

children.note: Acid soils (common in high-rainfall Kenya highlands and NE India) are corrected with agricultural lime. Alkaline and sodic soils may need gypsum and organic matter.
Electrical conductivity measures dissolved salts in soil. On Soil Health Cards, EC below 1 dS/m is normal; higher values can harm germination and sensitive crops.

manas.q: What does soil EC measure?

links.label: 📄 Source: Soil Health Card, Govt of India

children.note: Organic carbon is the main lab indicator of organic matter. Indian Soil Health Card ratings treat below 0.5% as low, 0.5–0.75% as medium and above 0.75% as high.

manas.q: On India's Soil Health Card, what organic carbon level is rated low?

links.label: 📄 Source: Soil Health Card, Govt of India

children.note: Labs report available nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, usually in kg/ha in India and mg/kg (ppm) in many other labs.
Commonly used ratings: available N low below 280, medium 280–560, high above 560 kg/ha; P (Olsen) low below 10, medium 10–25, high above 25; K low below 110, medium 110–280, high above 280 kg/ha.

links.label: 📄 Source: Soil Health Card, Govt of India

children.note: Phosphorus values depend on the extraction method, such as Olsen for neutral-alkaline soils or Bray/Mehlich for acid soils. Compare results only within the same method.
Labs can test sulphur, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, manganese, copper and boron. Zinc deficiency is widespread in Indian and Kenyan soils.
Commonly used critical limits by DTPA extraction are about 0.6 ppm zinc, 4.5 ppm iron and 0.2 ppm copper, and about 0.5 ppm hot-water-soluble boron. Below these, crops may respond to application.
Cation exchange capacity is the soil's ability to hold positively charged nutrients such as calcium, magnesium and potassium. Clay and organic matter raise CEC; sandy soils have low CEC.

manas.q: What does cation exchange capacity (CEC) tell you?

children.note: Texture (sand, silt, clay) shapes drainage and nutrient holding. Bulk density shows compaction; higher values mean fewer pores for air and roots.
Microbial biomass carbon measures the amount of living microbes in soil. It responds faster than total organic carbon to changes in management.
Respiration tests measure the burst of CO2 released when dried soil is re-wetted, showing how active microbes are. The Solvita CO2-burst test is one widely used method.
Higher CO2 release generally means more active biology and more nutrients being released from organic matter. Compare soils tested by the same lab and method.

manas.q: What does a soil respiration (CO2-burst) test measure?

children.note: Some labs offer active carbon (permanganate oxidisable carbon), enzyme activity, potentially mineralisable nitrogen and phospholipid fatty acid (PLFA) profiles. These are useful for tracking change over time.
A test is only as good as the sample. A sample must represent the field, so it is made by mixing many small cores.
Sample after harvest and before the next crop, at least two to three months after fertiliser or manure application. Sample the same field at the same time of year for comparisons.
Treat each field or uniform area separately and walk in a zig-zag pattern, taking 10–20 spots. Avoid bunds, field edges, manure heaps, trees, compost pits and waterlogged spots.

manas.q: How many spots are usually combined into one composite sample?

children.note: For field crops, take soil from the top 0–15 cm (plough layer). For orchards and deep-rooted crops, sample deeper layers such as 0–30 and 30–60 cm separately.

manas.q: What depth is sampled for most field crops?

children.note: Clear surface litter, dig a V-shaped pit to the sampling depth and slice a thin, even layer of soil from one side. This gives equal soil from every depth.
Mix all cores in a clean bucket or on a sheet, then divide into four, discard two opposite quarters and repeat until about half a kilo remains.
Dry the sample in shade, never in an oven or direct sun, and pack it in a clean cloth or plastic bag. Label with farmer name, field, crop history, depth and date.
For microbial tests, keep samples cool and send them quickly as advised by the lab, because microbes change in a hot bag. Do not mix with fertiliser bags or chemicals.
A soil report lists measured values with ratings and often fertiliser recommendations. Read it as a whole, not one number at a time.
If pH or salts are far from normal, fix them first, because they control how much any nutrient can be used.
Low organic carbon means low biological activity and poor nutrient holding. Plan compost, manure, cover crops and residue retention alongside fertiliser.
Use the ratings (low, medium, high) with the crop's needs to adjust doses. Medium or high ratings may allow reduced application.
Yield is limited by the nutrient in shortest supply, so a zinc or sulphur gap can waste added NPK. Fix the most limiting factor first.

manas.q: Why can a micronutrient deficiency waste NPK fertiliser?

children.note: One test is a snapshot; tests every two to three years from the same field show whether management is improving the soil.
Poor sampling, comparing results from different lab methods and acting on one number are the most common errors. Units such as ppm, mg/kg and kg/ha must not be mixed up.
Both countries have public and private soil testing networks. Farmers can often get tests at low cost through government programmes.
The Soil Health Card scheme gives farmers a card with test results and crop-wise fertiliser advice for their land. Samples are tested in state and district soil testing labs.

manas.q: What does India's Soil Health Card give farmers?

children.note: Krishi Vigyan Kendras, state agriculture departments and agricultural universities run soil testing labs and help farmers take samples. Some offer mobile testing vans.
The Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization runs soil and plant analysis services and research on soil fertility. County extension officers can advise on sampling.
Accredited private labs in Nairobi and other towns offer soil, plant tissue and water tests. Rapid in-field kits and scanners are spreading but should be checked against a lab.
Choose a lab that uses standard methods, explains its units and gives crop-specific advice. Use the same lab over time for comparable results.

nodeData.note: Plants show nutrient shortages through colour, shape and where on the plant the damage starts. Learning to read these signs, then confirming with a soil or leaf test, lets you choose the right compost, mineral or microbe instead of guessing.

children.topic: How to read a sick plant
children.note: A simple field routine: look at where symptoms start, what pattern they form, and how they are spread across the field before deciding it is a nutrient problem.
First note whether the lower, older leaves or the young top leaves and growing tips are affected. This single clue splits nutrients into two groups.

manas.q: What is the first question to ask when diagnosing a deficiency?

children.note: Is the whole leaf pale, is yellowing only between the veins, are the margins burnt, or are there spots? Each pattern points to different nutrients.
A nutrient problem is usually gradual and follows soil type or management. Sharp patches, rows or a single spray swath suggest disease, pests, drainage or chemical injury.
Note pH, drainage, organic matter and recent weather. Many 'deficiencies' are really lock-outs caused by pH, waterlogging or cold soil.
A soil test and, where available, a leaf (tissue) test confirm what the eye suspects. Treat visual diagnosis as a hypothesis, not a verdict.

manas.q: Why should visual diagnosis be confirmed with a soil or leaf test?

children.note: After correcting, new growth should look normal within some weeks. Old damaged leaves rarely recover, so judge by new leaves.

A nutrient that can move inside the plant is shifted from old leaves to new growth when in short supply, so old leaves show signs first. An immobile nutrient stays put, so new leaves and tips suffer first.
These move readily in the phloem. When short, the plant robs older leaves to feed new growth, so lower leaves yellow, purple or scorch first.

manas.q: Which major nutrients are mobile, so their deficiency shows first on older leaves?

children.note: Molybdenum is moderately mobile and its shortage often looks like nitrogen deficiency on older and middle leaves, because Mo is needed to use nitrogen.
Calcium and boron barely move once placed in a leaf. Shortage shows at growing tips, young leaves, roots and fruit (e.g. blossom-end rot).

manas.q: Why does calcium deficiency show at growing tips and fruit rather than old leaves?

children.topic: Low mobility: Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu
children.note: These micronutrients move poorly, so symptoms such as yellowing between veins or small leaves appear on the youngest leaves.
Sulfur moves only partly, so S shortage usually shows as pale young leaves. This helps separate it from N shortage, which yellows old leaves first.

manas.q: How can you tell sulfur from nitrogen deficiency by leaf position?

children.note: Old leaves: N, P, K, Mg (and Mo). New leaves: Ca, S, Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B. Learn this split before learning individual symptoms.
The three nutrients crops take up in the largest amounts and the most common shortages in tropical soils.
How Nitrogen shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Whole plant pale green; older leaves turn yellow from the tip, then brown and die. Growth is slow and plants may mature early.

manas.q: What does nitrogen deficiency look like?

children.note: Common on low-organic-matter soils, after heavy rain that leaches nitrate, and where residues are burnt. Waterlogging and cold soils can mimic it.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Add well-made compost or FYM, grow legumes or green manure, and use N-fixers: Rhizobium for legumes, Azotobacter or Azospirillum for cereals and vegetables. Biofertilizers supply part of the need, not all of it.
How Phosphorus shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Plants are stunted and dark, with older leaves taking a purple or reddish tint, often on the underside. Roots and early growth are weak; flowering and maturity are delayed.

manas.q: Which microbes help correct phosphorus shortage?

children.note: P is locked up in both acidic soils (by iron and aluminium) and calcareous soils (by calcium). Cold soil and some hybrids also show purple tints without true P shortage.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Rock phosphate mixed into compost, together with phosphate-solubilising bacteria (PSB) that release P using organic acids. Mycorrhizal (AM) fungi extend roots to reach more P.
How Potassium shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Edges of older leaves turn yellow then scorch brown, as if burnt. Stems are weak and lodge, and fruit and grain quality is poor.
Typical on sandy, leached or eroded soils and under intensive cropping with no K returned. Drought scorch and salt damage can look similar.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Return crop residues, apply wood ash (sparingly, it raises pH) and K-rich compost. Potassium-mobilising bacteria (KMB/KSB) help release K held in soil minerals.
Needed in moderate amounts. Calcium and magnesium shortages are tied to acidic or sodic soils; sulfur to low organic matter.
How Calcium shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Growing tips of roots and shoots brown and die, young leaves are ragged or hooked, and fruit develops blossom-end rot (tomato, pepper).

manas.q: Which disorder in tomato fruit is linked to calcium shortage?

children.note: Common on acidic soils, but often caused by uneven watering because Ca travels with water flow. High K or sodium can compete with it.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Agricultural lime (calcium carbonate) on acid soils, gypsum where pH need not rise, and steady irrigation and mulch to keep water flow even.
How Magnesium shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Older leaves yellow between the veins while the veins stay green, giving a striped or herringbone look; leaves may turn reddish later.

manas.q: What does dolomite supply besides raising pH?

children.note: Acid, leached soils and heavy potassium or ammonium use, which compete with Mg uptake. Can be confused with virus mosaic.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Dolomitic lime corrects both acidity and Mg on acid soils. Compost and well-rotted manure add some Mg; avoid excessive K.
How Sulfur shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Young leaves are uniformly pale green to yellow, plants are thin and spindly. Oilseeds and brassicas are especially sensitive.
Low-organic-matter soils, residue burning and long use of fertilisers without sulfur. Easily confused with N shortage, which hits old leaves first.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Gypsum, compost and FYM supply S. Sulfur-oxidising bacteria (e.g. Thiobacillus) turn elemental sulfur into a plant-available form.
Needed in tiny amounts but essential. Most show on young leaves and are strongly affected by soil pH.
How Iron shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Young leaves turn yellow between the veins with veins sharply green; in severe cases new growth bleaches almost white.

manas.q: Why is iron chlorosis usually a lock-out rather than a lack of iron in the soil?

children.note: Rarely a true shortage of iron in soil; usually lock-out on calcareous, high-pH or waterlogged soils.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Lower pH locally with compost and sulfur, improve drainage, and use organic matter. Siderophore-producing bacteria such as Pseudomonas help chelate iron.
How Zinc shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Upper leaves show interveinal yellowing turning whitish; leaves are small and bunched into a rosette. In rice it causes browning ('khaira').

manas.q: What is ZSB and which deficiency does it address?

children.note: Calcareous soils, high-P soils, eroded soils where topsoil is lost, and flooded rice soils.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Zinc-solubilising bacteria (ZSB) release zinc from native soil compounds. Compost and FYM help; certifier-approved zinc sulfate is used when the soil truly lacks Zn.
How Manganese shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Young leaves get yellowing between veins with a speckled or mottled look; grey speck in oats is a classic form.
High-pH and calcareous soils, and very high organic matter. On very acid soils Mn can instead be toxic.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Correct pH toward neutral, add compost, and avoid over-liming. Healthy root microbes and mycorrhiza support Mn uptake.
How Boron shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Growing points die, young leaves are thick and distorted, flowers and fruit drop, and stems or roots crack (hollow stem in cabbage, cracked fruit).

manas.q: Why must boron be applied with great care?

children.note: Sandy and leached soils, and alkaline soils with free lime. Drought makes it worse. The gap between deficient and toxic levels is narrow.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Compost and organic matter hold boron; only tiny, measured doses of approved borax should be added. Never guess boron rates.
How Copper shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Young leaves are pale, twisted or dieback at the tips; cereals may have white, twisted leaf tips and empty ears.
Peat and very high organic matter soils bind copper; also sandy leached soils.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Usually corrected with small approved copper doses on proven-deficient soils. Compost from mixed sources supplies traces.
How Molybdenum shortage shows up, what it is mistaken for, and the organic or biological way to correct it.
Looks like nitrogen deficiency: older and middle leaves pale, margins may cup; 'whiptail' in cauliflower.

manas.q: Which micronutrient becomes more available when soil pH rises?

children.note: Strongly acidic soils lock Mo up; it is the one micronutrient that becomes more available as pH rises.

links.label: 📄 Source: TNAU Agritech – conditions inducing deficiency

children.note: Liming acid soils often frees Mo. Legumes need Mo for Rhizobium to fix nitrogen, so poor nodulation can be a Mo signal.
Many problems mimic deficiencies. Rule these out before adding inputs.
Viral mosaics, wilts, root rots and leaf spots cause yellowing. Disease often shows lesions, spores, ooze, or a spreading patch rather than a symmetrical pattern.
Saturated soil starves roots of oxygen; plants yellow and wilt like N or Fe deficiency. Check drainage and smell for sour soil.
Dry soil stops nutrient flow to roots, causing leaf scorch like K shortage and calcium disorders in fruit.
The nutrient is present but unavailable because soil is too acid or too alkaline. Adding more fertiliser does little; fixing pH does.

manas.q: What is pH lock-out?

children.note: Twisted, cupped or strapped leaves, bleached new growth, or damage following a spray line or drift direction point to herbicide, not nutrition.

manas.q: What field clues suggest herbicide injury instead of deficiency?

children.note: Sucking pests cause stippling and bronzing; nematodes damage roots so plants look nutrient-starved. Check undersides of leaves and roots.
Hardpans, cutworms or transplant shock limit roots, so the plant cannot take up nutrients that are in the soil.
Too much fertiliser or saline water burns leaf edges and tips, looking like K deficiency.
The main organic and biological inputs, matched to the nutrient they support. They work best together with organic matter.
The base for every remedy: supply many nutrients slowly, feed soil microbes, improve water holding and buffer pH swings.
Legumes with Rhizobium add N; green manure crops add organic matter; Azolla with its cyanobacterial partner adds N in rice fields.
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria for non-legumes such as cereals, millets and vegetables. They also produce growth hormones.

manas.q: Which bacteria fix nitrogen for non-legume crops?

children.note: Phosphate-solubilising bacteria release acids that dissolve rock phosphate and soil P. Enriching compost with both is a common practice.
Potassium-mobilising bacteria release K from soil minerals. They help where soil K reserves exist but are slowly available.
Zinc-solubilising bacteria free zinc already present in the soil. They do not create zinc where the soil truly has none.
Root-partner fungi whose threads reach far beyond roots, improving uptake of P, Zn and water.

manas.q: How do mycorrhizal fungi improve phosphorus uptake?

children.note: Lime raises pH and adds Ca; dolomite adds Ca and Mg; gypsum adds Ca and S without raising pH.
A source of K and Ca that also raises pH. Use small amounts and avoid on alkaline soils.
Contain traces of nutrients and growth substances. They support plants under stress but do not correct a serious deficiency alone.
Common errors when farmers try to fix yellow plants.
Yellowing has many causes: S, Fe, Mg, waterlogging, disease. Adding N to a non-N problem wastes money and can worsen pests.
If pH or drainage is the cause, inputs keep failing. Fix the soil condition first.
Biofertilizers need organic matter, moisture and correct pH. They complement nutrition; they rarely replace it fully on poor soils.

manas.q: Can biofertilizers alone always fix a severe deficiency?

children.note: Applying bacteria with fungicides, copper sprays or concentrated fertilisers can kill them before they act.
Boron, copper and zinc become toxic at high rates. Test, then apply small measured doses.
Local context for using these signs and remedies.
Many Kenyan highland soils are acidic, so P lock-out and Ca/Mg shortages are common; liming with soil-test guidance is often the first step.
Zinc and sulfur shortages are widespread in Indian soils; Soil Health Card testing helps identify them.
In Kenya, KALRO and private labs test soils; in India, Soil Health Card labs and KVKs do. Base decisions on results.
Use registered biofertilizers and approved minerals; organic farms must check permitted inputs with their certifier or PGS group.

nodeData.note: Rhizobia are bacteria that form pink nodules on legume roots and fix air nitrogen for the plant. Using the right strain for each crop group, applied carefully on seed, can supply much of a legume's nitrogen.

children.note: Rhizobia are soil bacteria that live in partnership with legume plants and turn air nitrogen into a form the plant can use.
Rhizobia are rod-shaped, Gram-negative soil bacteria. On their own in soil they do little for nitrogen; their value comes when they enter a legume root.

manas.q: What type of organism is Rhizobium, and which plants does it partner with?

children.note: The group called rhizobia includes Rhizobium, Bradyrhizobium, Mesorhizobium and Sinorhizobium (also called Ensifer), among others. Each genus tends to suit different legume crops.

manas.q: Name four genera of rhizobia.

children.note: Unlike Azotobacter, rhizobia fix meaningful nitrogen only inside root nodules, where the plant supplies sugar and a low-oxygen home.

manas.q: Does Rhizobium fix useful nitrogen while free in the soil?

children.note: A given rhizobial strain nodulates only a certain set of legumes. That is why inoculants are sold per crop group, not as one product for every legume.
The legume and the bacterium exchange chemical signals, build a nodule together, and then trade sugar for fixed nitrogen.
Legume roots release flavonoids. Matching rhizobia answer with Nod factors, signal molecules that tell the root to start forming a nodule.

manas.q: What signal molecules do rhizobia send to the legume root?

children.topic: Root hair curl and infection thread
children.note: The root hair curls around the bacteria and a tube called the infection thread carries them inward to dividing root cells.
Inside the new nodule the bacteria change into bacteroids, the form that actually fixes nitrogen.
The enzyme nitrogenase converts air nitrogen into ammonia, which the plant builds into proteins. The process costs the plant a lot of energy.

manas.q: Which enzyme converts atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia in the nodule?

children.note: Nitrogenase is damaged by oxygen. The plant makes leghaemoglobin, a red pigment that binds oxygen and gives active nodules their pink colour.

manas.q: Why are active nodules pink inside?

children.note: In return for nitrogen the plant feeds the bacteroids with carbon from photosynthesis, so a healthy, well-lit crop supports better fixation.
Roots, nodules and residues of a well-nodulated legume leave some nitrogen in the soil, which helps a following cereal crop.
A cross-inoculation group is a set of legumes that can be nodulated by the same rhizobia. Use the inoculant made for your crop's group.
Legumes in one group share compatible rhizobia; an inoculant from another group usually forms few or no working nodules.

manas.q: What is a cross-inoculation group?

children.note: Soybean needs its own slow-growing Bradyrhizobium strains. Where soybean is new to a field, native soil rarely has them, so inoculation is especially important.

manas.q: Which rhizobium is used for soybean?

children.note: Chickpea (Bengal gram) is nodulated by Mesorhizobium strains specific to chickpea; it forms its own group.

manas.q: Which rhizobium group nodulates chickpea?

children.note: These share Rhizobium leguminosarum (biovar viciae), so one pea-group inoculant suits them.
French and common beans use bean-group strains such as R. phaseoli, R. etli and R. tropici. In Kenya, bean is the most widely inoculated legume.
Cowpea, groundnut, pigeonpea, green gram and black gram fall in the broad cowpea group, mostly nodulated by Bradyrhizobium.

manas.q: Name three crops in the cowpea cross-inoculation group.

children.note: Lucerne (alfalfa), fenugreek (methi) and sweet clover are nodulated by Sinorhizobium meliloti.
Clovers (Trifolium, incl. berseem) form a group with R. leguminosarum biovar trifolii.
TNAU lists approximate fixation of about 57–105 kg N/ha for soybean and cowpea-group crops, 75–117 for chickpea and 62–132 for pea and lentil, depending on conditions.
Checking nodules is the simplest way to know if Rhizobium is working. Dig, don't pull, and cut nodules open.
Dig up a few plants with soil around the roots at early flowering, wash gently in water and look at the crown of the main root.
Slice a nodule with a blade. A pink to red centre shows leghaemoglobin and active nitrogen fixation.

manas.q: What colour is the inside of an effective nodule?

children.topic: White, green or grey = not fixing
children.note: White insides mean the nodule is young or ineffective; green or grey means it is old or failing, often after drought or waterlogging.

manas.q: What does a white or green nodule interior indicate?

children.note: Large nodules clustered on the upper taproot usually come from the inoculant on the seed; small scattered ones on side roots are often native, less effective strains.
Soybean, bean and groundnut form round nodules; pea, chickpea and alfalfa form longer, finger-like or branched nodules. Both shapes can be effective.
Wrong or dead inoculant, hot or dry treated seed, acid soil, high fertilizer nitrogen, seed fungicide mixed with inoculant, or waterlogging.

manas.q: List three common reasons for poor or no nodulation.

children.note: Inoculate whenever a legume is new to a field, or past crops showed poor nodules or pale plants.
If the crop (or its group) has not been grown recently, matching rhizobia are probably absent and inoculation gives the biggest benefit.

manas.q: When is inoculating a legume most likely to pay off?

children.note: Uniform yellowing starting from older, lower leaves in a legume often means nodules are not supplying enough nitrogen.
Many pink nodules, dark green leaves without added nitrogen and vigorous growth through flowering and pod filling.
Acid soils, drought, waterlogging and very high soil temperatures reduce nodule formation and fixation.
When much mineral nitrogen is available, the plant forms fewer nodules. A small starter dose is fine; heavy urea defeats the purpose.

manas.q: What happens to nodulation when large amounts of nitrogen fertilizer are applied?

children.note: Nodules need phosphorus for energy, molybdenum for nitrogenase and calcium for infection. Deficient soils give weak fixation even with good inoculant.

manas.q: Which micronutrient is part of the nitrogenase enzyme?

children.note: Rhizobium inoculants are living products. Form, count and freshness matter more than the price.
Bacteria grown in a fine carrier such as peat or lignite. Cheap and common; mixed with a sticker and coated on seed.
Bacteria in a broth with protectants. Liquids are easier to dose, need less volume per acre and usually keep longer than powders.
Granular inoculants are placed in the seed furrow; useful when seed carries fungicide or is too delicate to coat.
TNAU notes carrier packets should hold above 10⁹ cells/g when made and at least 10⁷ cells/g up to expiry. Always check the count and the crop group printed on the pack.
TNAU gives roughly 12–24 months for liquid formulations; carrier packets are shorter-lived. Never use past the expiry date.
Keep packs in a cool, dry, shaded place away from heat and direct sun; never leave them in a hot vehicle or shop window.

manas.q: How should Rhizobium inoculant be stored?

children.note: In India biofertilizers must meet Fertiliser Control Order (FCO) standards. In Kenya, inoculants are regulated through KEPHIS and related bodies; buy registered products only.
Seed coating is the standard way to apply Rhizobium. Work in the shade and sow the same day.
Boil a little jaggery (gur) or rice gruel in water and let it cool fully. Hot sticker kills the bacteria.

manas.q: What is jaggery or rice gruel used for in seed inoculation?

children.note: Stir the inoculant into the cool sticker to make an even slurry. TNAU's carrier method uses one 200 g packet in 200 ml rice gruel.
Spread seed on a clean sheet or in a bag and mix with the slurry by hand until every seed has a thin coat, without breaking seed coats.
Air-dry the coated seed in shade for about half an hour. Sunlight and heat quickly kill rhizobia.

manas.q: Why must inoculated seed be dried in shade, not sun?

children.note: Sow within a few hours, and not later than 24 hours, into moist soil and cover it promptly.
TNAU suggests about 200 ml liquid per acre of pulse seed, or one 200 g carrier packet per about 10 kg seed. Follow the product label.
If seed must be treated with fungicide, apply it first, let it dry, then inoculate just before sowing; never mix them in one slurry.

manas.q: If seed needs fungicide, in what order are fungicide and Rhizobium applied?

children.note: Rhizobium can be combined with phosphate-solubilising bacteria; TNAU advises Rhizobium on the seed first and PSB as the outer layer.
Living bacteria die from heat, sun, chemicals and time.
Do not mix inoculant with chemical fertilizers, insecticides, fungicides or herbicides.
Keep treated seed and packs out of the sun and sow into moist soil so bacteria survive until roots emerge.

children.topic: Use the whole pack at once
children.note: Once opened, a pack starts losing viable bacteria; use it the same day.
In acid soils, a fine coat of lime or rock phosphate over inoculated seed helps protect rhizobia.
Well-decomposed FYM or compost supports soil biology and does not harm the inoculant.
Good inoculation can supply much of a legume's own nitrogen needs and leave some for the next crop, but results vary with soil and season.
A well-nodulated legume usually needs little or no extra nitrogen beyond a small starter dose.
Responses are strongest in fields new to the crop; where native strains are plentiful, gains may be small.

children.topic: Not a substitute for P and K
children.note: Rhizobium supplies only nitrogen. Phosphorus, potassium, sulphur and micronutrients still need managing.
Cereals after a good legume crop often grow better thanks to residual nitrogen and improved soil.
Most failures come from handling, not from the bacteria.

children.topic: Myth: one inoculant for all legumes
children.note: Strains are group-specific. Soybean inoculant will not help chickpea, and the reverse.

children.topic: Mistake: checking too early or late
children.note: Very young plants have tiny nodules and old plants have spent ones. Check around early flowering.
Heavy nitrogen fertilizer makes the plant stop forming nodules, so it wastes both the inoculant and the urea.

children.topic: Myth: lots of nodules means success
children.note: Many small white nodules may fix nothing. Colour inside matters more than number.

nodeData.note: Azotobacter is a free-living, aerobic soil bacterium that fixes nitrogen and releases growth hormones near roots of non-legume crops. It works best in soils rich in organic matter and complements, not replaces, good fertility.

children.note: Azotobacter is a free-living, aerobic soil bacterium that fixes nitrogen without forming nodules.
It fixes nitrogen while living freely in soil and around roots, and it needs oxygen to live.

manas.q: Is Azotobacter symbiotic or free-living, and does it need oxygen?

children.note: The most common species in farm soils and the one most used in biofertilizers. Its cultures turn brown to black with age.

manas.q: Which Azotobacter species is most common in arable soils and biofertilizers?

children.note: A closely related species widely studied in laboratories; it has backup nitrogenases that can work when molybdenum is scarce.

manas.q: Which Azotobacter species is known for alternative (vanadium) nitrogenases?

children.note: Cells are large, oval rods that often occur in pairs and produce plenty of slime.
It is common in the soil around roots (rhizosphere) but does not enter root tissue or form nodules.

manas.q: Does Azotobacter form root nodules?

children.note: As it cannot make its own food, it depends on organic matter and root exudates; poor, low-carbon soils hold few cells.
Azotobacter helps plants mainly through nitrogen fixation and plant growth substances.
Like rhizobia it uses nitrogenase to turn N₂ into ammonia, but it does so on its own using soil carbon for energy.
It breathes very fast, using up oxygen inside the cell so the oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase can keep working.

manas.q: How does aerobic Azotobacter protect nitrogenase from oxygen?

children.note: Under stress it forms thick-walled cysts that resist drying; they germinate into active cells when moisture and food return.

manas.q: What resting structure does Azotobacter form to survive drought?

children.note: It releases growth substances such as indole acetic acid (an auxin), gibberellins and cytokinins that encourage root growth and germination.

manas.q: Name three plant growth hormones produced by Azotobacter.

children.note: B vitamins and other compounds it releases support seedling vigour and root branching.
Its polysaccharide slime (alginate) helps bind soil particles into aggregates.
TNAU notes Azotobacter produces substances that inhibit several soil fungi, a minor protective effect.
Azotobacter is meant for non-legume crops.
Wheat, maize, barley, oats, sorghum, pearl and finger millet respond to seed treatment.
Tomato, brinjal, chilli, cabbage, cauliflower, onion and others, by seedling root dip or soil application.
Cotton, mustard, sunflower, sesame and castor are listed crops for seed treatment.
Sugarcane setts, tea, coffee, coconut, fruit trees and nursery plants via soil or sett treatment.
Useful in nurseries and upland rice; in flooded paddy, Azospirillum and blue-green algae are generally preferred.
For pulses and soybeans, Rhizobium is the main nitrogen inoculant; Azotobacter is not a substitute.

manas.q: Should Azotobacter replace Rhizobium for legumes?

children.note: Azotobacter does best in well-aerated, near-neutral soils rich in organic matter.
Without enough organic carbon the bacteria cannot multiply; pair it with compost or FYM.

manas.q: What soil condition most limits Azotobacter numbers?

children.note: It performs poorly in strongly acidic soils; liming or Azospirillum may be better there.

manas.q: How does Azotobacter cope with acidic soils?

children.note: Moist but not waterlogged soil suits it; prolonged flooding limits this aerobic organism.
Low-input or organic fields, crops showing pale older leaves from nitrogen shortage, and soils low in biological activity.
There is no nodule to inspect; look for better germination, stronger roots and greener growth than untreated strips.

manas.q: How can a farmer judge if Azotobacter is working, since it forms no nodules?

children.note: Sold as carrier powder, liquid, granules, or in NPK consortia.
Bacteria in lignite or similar carrier; mixed with sticker for seed or with compost for soil.
Broth with protectants; easier dosing. TNAU gives roughly 12–24 months shelf life for liquids.
Ready for broadcasting or furrow application with manure.
Combined with phosphate-solubilising and potash-mobilising bacteria in one product for broad nutrient support.
Check the viable count, species, crop list and expiry on the pack; India's FCO sets minimum counts for sale.
Keep cool, dry and shaded, away from sun and chemicals; never use after expiry.

manas.q: How should Azotobacter products be stored?

children.note: India: FCO biofertilizer standards. Kenya: products should be registered with the relevant authorities (e.g. KEPHIS); avoid unlabelled products.
Choose seed, seedling or soil application by crop; work in shade and keep away from chemicals.
Mix inoculant with a cooled jaggery or rice gruel sticker, coat seed, dry in shade and sow the same day.
TNAU lists about 200 ml liquid per acre for seed treatment of wheat, millets, oilseeds and forage grasses.
For transplanted vegetables, dip roots in a suspension of inoculant in water for a short time before planting.
Mix with well-rotted FYM or compost, keep moist in shade for a few days, then spread before sowing or along rows.

manas.q: Why is Azotobacter mixed with compost or FYM for soil application?

children.note: Liquid can go through drip; TNAU lists about 2–3 ml per plant for coconut, fruit and nursery plants.
Apply at sowing or planting so bacteria establish with young roots; repeat soil application in long-duration crops if advised.
Do not mix with chemical fertilizers, fungicides or bactericides; separate by several days and apply fungicide first on seed.

manas.q: Can Azotobacter be mixed directly with chemical fungicides?

children.note: Azotobacter is a supplement that supports nitrogen supply and root growth, not a full replacement for fertilizer.
It can contribute some of the crop's nitrogen, so part of mineral N may be reduced; responses vary with soil carbon.
Trials commonly report modest yield improvements, mostly from hormone-driven root growth plus nitrogen.
TNAU notes Indian soils rarely hold more than about 10⁵ Azotobacter per gram, which is why inoculation can help.
Results are best where compost, mulches and residues feed soil life.
Common errors that waste the product.
It fixes far less than a legume–Rhizobium partnership; crops still need balanced nutrition.

manas.q: Does Azotobacter fully replace nitrogen fertilizer?

children.note: Without organic matter the bacteria starve; always add compost or manure.
Tank-mixing with fungicides or fertilizers kills the bacteria.
Heat and sun kill cells on treated seed; dry in shade and sow quickly.
Old or heat-exposed products may contain few living cells.

nodeData.note: Nitrogen-fixing helpers for non-legume crops: Azospirillum on cereal roots, Gluconacetobacter inside sugarcane, and cyanobacteria and Azolla in rice fields. They supply part of the crop's nitrogen and improve rooting.

children.topic: The big idea: N for non-legumes
children.note: Legumes get nitrogen from Rhizobium nodules, but cereals, millets and sugarcane have no nodules. A group of bacteria and cyanobacteria can still fix air nitrogen near, on or inside these crops.
Grasses such as maize, rice and sugarcane are heavy nitrogen feeders and depend almost entirely on soil and fertilizer N. Associative and free-living fixers add a modest extra supply.

manas.q: Why do cereals benefit from Azospirillum when they have no nodules?

children.topic: Three ways to live with a plant
children.note: Associative fixers (Azospirillum) live on and in roots; endophytes (Gluconacetobacter) live inside plant tissue; free-living cyanobacteria fix N in flood water. Azolla hosts Anabaena as a true symbiont.

manas.q: Name the lifestyle of Azospirillum, Gluconacetobacter and Anabaena in Azolla.

children.note: The enzyme that fixes nitrogen, nitrogenase, is damaged by oxygen. Each organism protects it differently: Azospirillum prefers low-oxygen zones and cyanobacteria fix N in thick-walled heterocysts.

manas.q: Which enzyme fixes nitrogen, and what damages it?

children.note: These organisms supply part of the crop's N and improve roots. They work alongside compost, manure and reduced fertilizer, not as a full substitute in most fields.
A soil bacterium that colonises the root surface and outer root tissue of grasses and cereals. It is one of the most widely used biofertilizers for non-legume crops in India.
Azospirillum brasilense and Azospirillum lipoferum are the species most used in inoculants. Both are Gram-negative, motile, curved rod-shaped bacteria.

manas.q: Which two Azospirillum species are most common in biofertilizers?

children.note: It does not form nodules. It lives in close association with roots, in the rhizosphere and in spaces of the root cortex, feeding on root exudates.

manas.q: Does Azospirillum form root nodules?

children.note: It fixes nitrogen best where oxygen is low but not absent, such as the root surface and moist soil. It swims toward roots using flagella.

manas.q: What does microaerophilic mean for Azospirillum?

children.note: It helps the crop in two ways: fixing some atmospheric nitrogen and, often more importantly, producing hormones that build a bigger root system.

children.topic: Fixes nitrogen in the root zone
children.note: It converts air nitrogen into ammonium that partly becomes available to the plant. TNAU cites about 20–40 kg N/ha for non-legume crops under good conditions.

manas.q: Roughly how much N can Azospirillum supply (TNAU)?

children.note: It releases indole-acetic acid, gibberellins and other growth substances. These cause more root hairs and lateral roots.

manas.q: Which plant hormone is Azospirillum best known for producing?

children.note: A larger root system takes up more water, phosphorus and micronutrients. This root effect explains much of its yield benefit.
Better-rooted plants cope better with short dry spells. TNAU also mentions improved drought tolerance and some disease resistance.

children.topic: Sign it is needed: yellow older leaves
children.note: Nitrogen shortage shows first as pale yellowing of older, lower leaves, often in a V-shape from the tip in maize. Growth is slow and thin.

manas.q: Where does N-deficiency yellowing appear first?

children.note: Expect stronger, hairier roots and steady green colour, not an overnight change. Compare treated and untreated strips in the same field.
Best suited to grasses and cereals, with reported use on a range of other non-legume crops.
These are the classic Azospirillum crops. Finger millet, pearl millet and sorghum respond well in low-input farming.

manas.q: Name four classic crops for Azospirillum.

children.note: Used for wheat and barley, often together with or instead of Azotobacter.
TNAU lists cotton and oilseeds; in South India it is also used on sugarcane together with phosphate solubilizers.
Relevant to maize, sorghum, millet and irrigated rice schemes. Use only registered products and test on a small area first.
An N-fixing bacterium that lives inside sugarcane. It was first described as Acetobacter diazotrophicus and later renamed Gluconacetobacter diazotrophicus.
Older labels say Acetobacter diazotrophicus; the current name is Gluconacetobacter diazotrophicus. Both refer to the same organism.

manas.q: What is the current name of Acetobacter diazotrophicus?

children.note: It lives inside the plant: in roots, stems and leaves of sugarcane. Being inside protects it from competition with soil microbes.

manas.q: Is Gluconacetobacter an endophyte or a soil free-living bacterium?

children.note: It thrives in sugary, acidic conditions like cane sap, which few other bacteria tolerate. That makes sugarcane its natural home.

manas.q: Why is sugarcane a good home for Gluconacetobacter?

children.note: Mainly sugarcane; also found in sweet sorghum and sweet potato.
Some Brazilian sugarcane varieties obtain part of their N from biological fixation, and Gluconacetobacter was found studying them. Benefits elsewhere depend on variety and conditions.
Usually by soaking setts in the bacterial suspension before planting, plus soil application with well-rotted FYM. Follow the label for dose and soaking time.
Some sources quote large yield and sugar gains; results in farmer fields vary. Treat it as one part of cane nutrition, not a stand-alone N source.
Photosynthetic bacteria that fix nitrogen in flooded rice fields. Using them as a biofertilizer is called algalization.
Despite the name, blue-green algae are cyanobacteria. They make their own food from sunlight and many also fix nitrogen.

manas.q: Are blue-green algae true algae?

children.note: Thick-walled special cells called heterocysts keep oxygen out so nitrogenase can work. Anabaena and Nostoc form chains with these cells.

manas.q: What is a heterocyst?

children.note: Nostoc, Anabaena, Aulosira and Tolypothrix are common in rice-field inocula. Composite starter cultures mix several species.

manas.q: Name two cyanobacteria genera used in rice.

children.note: Standing water, sunlight and neutral to slightly alkaline soil favour them. They are mainly a lowland rice technology.
They add organic matter, bind soil particles and release growth substances. They have also been used in salt-affected rice soils.
TNAU advises about 10 kg/ha of dried flakes mixed with 10 kg soil or sand, broadcast 7–10 days after transplanting.
Hold 3–4 inches of water for about a month after application so the algae can multiply.
TNAU reports about 20–30 kg N/ha under ideal conditions.

children.topic: Make your own: tray or field
children.note: Fill a shallow tray or small bunded plot with rice soil and water, add starter culture and a little superphosphate. After about two weeks, dry and collect the flakes.
Azolla is a tiny floating water fern that houses the cyanobacterium Anabaena azollae in its leaves. Together they fix nitrogen and serve as green manure for rice.
Anabaena azollae lives in cavities of Azolla leaves and passes fixed nitrogen to the fern. It is passed on from one generation of the fern to the next.

manas.q: Which cyanobacterium lives inside Azolla leaves?

children.note: Azolla pinnata is widespread in Asia; Azolla filiculoides and others are also used.
Under good conditions it can double its mass in a few days, covering the water surface as a green mat.
Grow and incorporate fresh Azolla before transplanting; TNAU cites about 15 t/ha of fresh biomass.
Broadcast about 500 kg/ha fresh Azolla 7 days after transplanting and trample it in as it grows.

manas.q: When is Azolla added as a dual crop in rice (TNAU)?

children.note: TNAU reports about 40–60 kg N/ha per rice crop.
A small bunded plot with 10 cm water, cow dung slurry and a little superphosphate grows a harvest in 2–3 weeks.
The thick mat shades out some weeds. Azolla is also fed to cattle, poultry and fish.
Heat, strong sun, drying out, low phosphorus and insect pests slow it. It suits fields with assured water.
A filamentous actinomycete bacterium that forms N-fixing root nodules on certain non-legume trees and shrubs.
Plants nodulated by Frankia are called actinorhizal. Casuarina and alder (Alnus) are the best-known hosts.

manas.q: Which bacterium nodulates Casuarina?

children.note: Mainly relevant to agroforestry, windbreaks and land reclamation, not field crops.

Concentrated bacteria in liquid with protective additives. TNAU gives a shelf life of about 12–24 months.

manas.q: Minimum cells/g in a carrier packet before expiry (TNAU)?

children.note: Mixtures of N-fixers, phosphate solubilizers and potash mobilizers in one pack. Convenient, but check each organism's count.
BGA is sold or made as dry soil-based flakes; Azolla is used fresh from a nursery.
Keep cool, dry and out of direct sun. Heat kills the bacteria faster than anything else.
Methods for Azospirillum and Gluconacetobacter; BGA and Azolla methods are in their own branches.
Mix the product with cooled rice gruel or jaggery solution, coat seeds evenly and dry in shade before sowing. TNAU suggests 200 ml liquid per acre of seed.
Dip seedling roots in a suspension (TNAU: two packets in 40 L water) for 5–10 minutes before transplanting.
Mix with well-rotted farmyard manure or compost, keep moist in shade overnight, then apply in furrows or at last ploughing.
Soak setts in a suspension of Gluconacetobacter or Azospirillum before planting, following the label.
Liquid products can go through drip lines; flush the system first and avoid mixing with chlorine or chemicals.
Do not mix with chemical fungicides, bactericides or strong fertilizers. If seed must be fungicide-treated, use a compatible one and apply bacteria last, or use soil application.

manas.q: Should Azospirillum be mixed with chemical fungicide?

children.note: Only conservative, well-established outcomes are listed here.
TNAU reports that Azospirillum can save about 25–30% of N fertilizer. Treat this as an upper guide, not a promise.

manas.q: How much N fertilizer can Azospirillum save (TNAU)?

children.note: Better roots and early vigour are the most consistent effects; yield gains in trials are usually modest.
Soil type, organic matter, moisture, strain quality and handling all change the response. Poor products give no effect.
Common errors and regulatory notes for India and Kenya.
No biofertilizer can feed a high-yield cereal crop alone. Use it to reduce, not eliminate, other N sources.
High doses of mineral N suppress biological nitrogen fixation, so bacteria add little.

children.note: Leaving treated seed or packs in the sun, or using expired stock, kills the bacteria.

nodeData.note: Soil bacteria and fungi that release phosphorus locked up as calcium, iron or aluminium phosphates. Used with compost and rock phosphate, they help crops get more from the phosphorus already in the soil.

children.topic: Why P gets locked in soil
children.note: Most soils hold plenty of total phosphorus, but only a tiny fraction is dissolved and available to roots at any time. Applied phosphate fertilizer is also quickly tied up.
Soil may contain hundreds of kg of P per hectare, yet roots can only take up phosphate dissolved in soil water, which is a very small share.

manas.q: Why can a soil rich in total P still be P-deficient?

children.note: In calcareous and alkaline soils, phosphate binds with calcium to form poorly soluble calcium phosphates.

manas.q: Which element locks P in alkaline soils?

children.note: In acid soils, common in Kenyan highlands and parts of India, phosphate binds tightly to iron and aluminium.

manas.q: Which elements lock P in acid soils?

children.note: A large part of soil P is in organic matter (e.g. phytate) and must be broken down by enzymes before plants can use it.
Phosphorus is most available around slightly acid to neutral pH (about 6–7). Liming acid soils and adding organic matter help.
Much of the phosphate from DAP or SSP is converted to insoluble forms within weeks, so crops use only part of it in the year applied.
Soil bacteria that release locked phosphate into forms roots can absorb. In India they are often sold as phosphobacteria.
A spore-forming bacterium; the variety phosphaticum is a classic PSB inoculant. Spores give it good survival in products.

manas.q: Which Bacillus species is the classic PSB inoculant?

children.note: A non-spore-forming PSB widely used in Indian inoculants.

manas.q: Name a Pseudomonas species used as PSB.

children.note: Bacillus subtilis, Bacillus circulans and other Pseudomonas strains also solubilise phosphate.
PSB are free-living, not symbiotic. They live in the rhizosphere where root exudates feed them.
Some soil fungi dissolve phosphate even more strongly than bacteria because they produce large amounts of organic acid.
A common black mould that produces citric and other acids; well studied for dissolving rock phosphate.

manas.q: Which Aspergillus species is a well-known phosphate solubilizer?

children.note: Listed by TNAU among phosphate-solubilizing fungi.
Penicillium strains (e.g. P. bilaiae in some countries) are used as phosphate-solubilizing inoculants.
Mycorrhizal fungi mainly extend roots to reach more phosphate; PSF dissolve it. Both can be used together.
Microbes use acids, enzymes and chelation to free phosphate.
They release gluconic, citric, oxalic and other acids that dissolve calcium phosphates and lower pH around the root.

manas.q: Name two organic acids PSB produce.

children.note: Organic acid anions grab iron, aluminium or calcium ions, freeing the phosphate that was bound to them.

manas.q: How do organic acids free P from iron and aluminium?

children.note: Enzymes such as phosphatases and phytase cut phosphate off organic compounds, mineralising organic P.

manas.q: Which enzymes release P from organic matter?

children.note: Many PSB also produce plant hormones and improve root growth, which adds to their benefit.
Rock phosphate is a cheap, natural, slow-release P source allowed in organic farming. PSB and organic matter help make it available.
It is mostly insoluble calcium phosphate, so it releases P slowly, especially in neutral or alkaline soils.

manas.q: Why is rock phosphate slow to release P?

children.note: Natural soil acidity dissolves rock phosphate more readily; in alkaline soils it needs microbial and organic help.
Mixing rock phosphate into compost heaps with PSB lets acids from decomposition dissolve it. The result is often called phosphorus-enriched compost.
TNAU suggests mixing 200 ml PSB with 400–600 kg cow dung/FYM and half a bag of rock phosphate, keeping it in shade overnight.

children.topic: Field signs: does the crop need P?
children.note: Recognise phosphorus shortage before reaching for any input; confirm with a soil test.
Older leaves turn dark green with purple or reddish tints, especially in maize and young seedlings in cold weather.

manas.q: What leaf colour signals P deficiency in maize?

children.note: Plants stay small with weak root systems and slow early growth.
P shortage delays flowering, seed set and maturity, and reduces grain filling.
Legumes short of P form fewer, smaller nodules and fix less nitrogen.

manas.q: How does P shortage affect legume nodulation?

children.note: Leaf colour can also come from cold, root damage or other nutrients. A soil test (Olsen or Bray P) confirms P status.
Better early vigour and rooting compared with an untreated strip. Effects are gradual and most visible where soil P is locked.
PSB suit almost all crops because every crop needs phosphorus.
Cereals, pulses, oilseeds, vegetables, sugarcane and fruit trees can be treated. TNAU recommends PSB for all crops.
Phosphorus drives nodulation, so PSB plus Rhizobium is a common pulse package.
Many Kenyan highland soils fix P strongly to Fe and Al. Combine PSB with lime, manure and P fertilizer or rock phosphate.
Where soluble P fertilizers are not allowed, PSB with rock phosphate and compost is a main P strategy.
Generic product types; quality and freshness decide results.
PSB in a carrier such as lignite. Low cost and easy for seed coating.
Longer shelf life; TNAU gives about 12–24 months for liquid biofertilizers.
TNAU looks for above 10⁹ cells/g at production and at least 10⁷ cells/g before expiry for carrier products.
PSB combined with N-fixers and potash mobilizers in one product.
PSB carried on granules or added to compost and organic manures for soil application.
Keep in a cool, shaded, dry place; never in sun or near chemicals. Respect the expiry date.
PSB are applied the same ways as other bacterial biofertilizers.
Coat seed using a sticker such as rice gruel or jaggery, dry in shade and sow soon. TNAU: 200 ml liquid per acre of seed.
When seeds get both an N-fixer and PSB, coat with Rhizobium/Azospirillum first and PSB as the outer layer.

manas.q: Which goes on the seed last: Rhizobium or PSB?

children.note: Dip roots in a PSB suspension before transplanting; TNAU advises at least half an hour.
Mix with well-rotted manure or compost (with rock phosphate if available), keep moist overnight in shade, then apply in rows or at land levelling.
Liquid PSB can be applied by drip after flushing lines; avoid tank mixes with chemicals.
Keep away from chemical fungicides, bactericides and direct contact with concentrated fertilizers. Moist soil with organic matter helps them survive.
Conservative expectations only.

children.topic: Better use of soil and fertilizer P
children.note: PSB can increase the share of soil and applied P that crops take up. They do not create phosphorus, so very P-poor soils still need P inputs.

manas.q: Can PSB create phosphorus in a soil with none?

children.note: Trials commonly report modest yield gains; responses vary with soil pH, organic matter and product quality.
Responses are most reliable where PSB are applied with compost or manure, which feeds them.
Avoid these common problems.
