nodeData.note: Soil bacteria that unlock potassium, zinc, sulphur, silicon and iron already present in soil or minerals. They complement fertilisers and work best with organic matter and moisture.

children.note: A group of soil bacteria that do not add new nutrients but help release potassium, zinc, sulphur, silicon and iron that are already in the soil or in applied minerals.
Unlike nitrogen fixers, these microbes cannot create nutrients from air. They unlock nutrients locked in minerals, insoluble salts or organic matter so roots can absorb them.

manas.q: Do K, Zn and S microbes create new nutrients?

children.note: The common products contain free-living rhizosphere bacteria that live around roots and in soil, not inside plant nodules.
Many soils hold large total amounts of potassium and zinc, but only a small part is in a form roots can take up at any moment. Microbes help shift some of the locked pool into the available pool.
Potassium solubilising or mobilising bacteria release potassium from soil minerals such as micas and feldspars.
A Gram-negative bacterium widely sold in India as a potash mobilising biofertilizer, used in crops such as tea and sugarcane.

manas.q: Name a Gram-negative bacterium sold in India as a potash mobiliser.

children.note: Formerly called Bacillus mucilaginosus, this spore-forming bacterium coats itself in slime and weathers silicate minerals to release potassium. TNAU lists a potash strain of it.

manas.q: What is the newer name of Bacillus mucilaginosus?

children.note: Strains of Bacillus edaphicus, other Bacillus species, Pseudomonas and some fungi such as Aspergillus can also release potassium in lab and pot studies.
They release organic acids (such as citric, oxalic and gluconic acid) and slimy polysaccharides that dissolve and chelate the mineral surface, freeing potassium ions.

manas.q: What main chemical tool do KSB use to free potassium?

children.note: Most soil potassium sits inside mineral crystals. A smaller share is held on clay surfaces and only a tiny share is dissolved in soil water where roots can take it.
ZSB turn insoluble zinc compounds in soil, such as zinc oxide, carbonate and phosphate, into forms plants can absorb.
Mostly Bacillus and Pseudomonas strains, with some Gluconacetobacter and other rhizosphere bacteria. TNAU lists Bacillus as a silicate and zinc solubiliser.
They lower pH near roots by releasing acids (gluconic acid is common) and protons, and they make chelating compounds that keep zinc dissolved.

manas.q: Which organic acid is commonly linked with zinc solubilisation?

children.note: Zinc deficiency is common in alkaline, calcareous, sandy or eroded soils, in soils with very high phosphate, and in flooded rice fields.
ZSB work best when some zinc is present, for example native soil zinc or low-cost zinc oxide or zinc carbonate added to soil.
These bacteria convert elemental sulphur and other reduced sulphur forms into sulphate, the form plants take up.
Classic sulphur oxidisers. Thiobacillus thiooxidans is now named Acidithiobacillus thiooxidans; other Thiobacillus and many heterotrophic bacteria also oxidise sulphur.

manas.q: What is the current genus name for Thiobacillus thiooxidans?

children.note: They gain energy by oxidising sulphur to sulphuric acid. This supplies sulphate and slightly acidifies the zone around the sulphur particle.
They need a sulphur source to act on. They are typically paired with elemental sulphur, sulphur-coated products or gypsum-poor soils that receive sulphur.
The acid they produce can locally lower pH, which may improve availability of phosphorus and micronutrients in alkaline or sodic soils when enough sulphur is added.
Bacteria, mostly Bacillus species, that release silicon and other nutrients from silicate minerals.
Silicon is not essential for most crops but is beneficial, especially for rice and sugarcane. It strengthens cell walls, helps leaves stand upright and can reduce lodging and some pest attack.

manas.q: Which two crops benefit most from silicon?

children.note: Like KSB, they use organic acids and slimes to weather silicate minerals. One organism often releases both potassium and silicon.
Some bacteria help plants get iron and also starve pathogens of it by producing siderophores.
A small molecule that microbes release to grab ferric iron (Fe3+) very tightly. The iron-siderophore complex is then taken up by the microbe and sometimes by plants.

manas.q: What is a siderophore?

children.note: Pseudomonas fluorescens and related species make strong siderophores (pyoverdines). This is one reason they also act as biocontrol agents.
By locking up iron, siderophore producers can deprive root pathogens such as Fusarium and Pythium of iron, slowing their growth.

manas.q: How can siderophores help suppress root disease?

children.note: Knowing which leaves show symptoms first helps you tell nutrient problems apart. Confirm with a soil or leaf test before acting.
Yellowing then browning and scorching along the edges and tips of older, lower leaves, because K moves to new growth. Weak stems, lodging and poor fruit or grain fill follow.

manas.q: Where does potassium deficiency show first, and how?

children.note: Shows on young leaves: pale stripes or patches between veins, small narrow leaves, short internodes and a bunched rosette look. In maize it appears as white or pale bands near the leaf base.

manas.q: What are typical zinc deficiency signs?

children.note: A zinc deficiency disorder of rice in India: rusty brown spots on older leaves a few weeks after transplanting, with stunted, patchy growth.

manas.q: Which nutrient deficiency causes khaira disease in rice?

children.note: Even pale yellowing of the whole plant, often starting on younger leaves, because S moves less within the plant. It is easily confused with nitrogen deficiency, which starts on older leaves.

manas.q: How do you tell S deficiency from N deficiency?

manas.q: Why mix soil-applied biofertilizer with compost or FYM?

manas.q: What should not be mixed with bacterial biofertilizers?

nodeData.note: Soil fungi that partner with plant roots, extending them with fine hyphae to bring in phosphorus, zinc and water in exchange for plant sugars. Most crops benefit; protecting native fungi matters as much as adding inoculum.

children.note: Mycorrhiza means 'fungus-root': a partnership in which a soil fungus lives with plant roots and trades nutrients and water for plant sugars.
The plant feeds the fungus with sugars and fats made by photosynthesis. In return the fungus delivers phosphorus, other nutrients and water from soil the roots cannot reach.

manas.q: What does each partner give in a mycorrhizal symbiosis?

children.note: Arbuscular mycorrhiza (AM) is found in most crops. Ectomycorrhiza is found mainly in forest trees such as pines and eucalyptus.
Fossils show this relationship dates back to the first land plants, which is why so many plant families carry it.
AMF grow inside root cortex cells and form tree-like structures called arbuscules. Older texts call them VAM (vesicular-arbuscular mycorrhiza).
Key genera are Rhizophagus (R. irregularis, formerly Glomus intraradices), Funneliformis (formerly Glomus mosseae), Glomus, Gigaspora and Acaulospora. Glomus is the most common.

manas.q: What is the current name of Glomus intraradices?

children.note: AMF belong to their own fungal group, the Glomeromycota. They do not form mushrooms.
Finely branched structures inside root cells where nutrients and sugars are exchanged.

manas.q: What are arbuscules?

children.note: Swollen, fat-filled sacs inside roots that act as food stores for the fungus.
Large, thick-walled resting spores formed in soil or roots. They survive dry seasons and start new colonies.
AMF cannot complete their life without a living host root, so they cannot be grown on lab media like bacteria. This makes inoculum harder to produce.

manas.q: Why is AMF inoculum harder to produce than bacterial biofertilizers?

children.note: In ectomycorrhiza the fungus wraps the root tip in a sheath and grows between, not into, root cells.
The fungal sheath around short roots is the mantle. The web of hyphae between outer root cells is the Hartig net, where exchange takes place.

manas.q: What are the two key structures of ectomycorrhiza?

children.note: Mainly pines, eucalyptus, oaks, birch and other forest trees. Many common forest mushrooms are the fruiting bodies of these fungi.
Pisolithus, Laccaria, Suillus, Rhizopogon and many others. Some are used in forestry nurseries.
Pines planted in new regions often grow poorly until their ectomycorrhizal partners are introduced, so nurseries inoculate seedlings.

children.topic: AM vs ecto at a glance
children.note: AM: inside cells, most crops, no mushrooms. Ecto: outside cells with a sheath, mostly trees, often produces mushrooms.

manas.q: How do AM and ectomycorrhiza differ?

children.note: The fungus acts like a giant extension of the root system.
Fungal threads are much finer than roots and grow several centimetres beyond them, exploring far more soil volume per gram of plant carbon.
Phosphate moves very slowly in soil, so roots quickly empty the soil next to them. Hyphae reach past this depleted zone and bring P back.

manas.q: Why are mycorrhizae especially good at improving P uptake?

children.note: AMF also improve uptake of other slow-moving nutrients, notably zinc and copper, and help with sulphur and nitrogen.
Hyphae enter fine soil pores roots cannot reach and keep supplying water as soil dries.
Hyphae can link neighbouring plants underground. How much they share resources is still being studied.
AMF help build stable soil crumbs.
A sticky glycoprotein linked to AMF hyphae, measured as glomalin-related soil protein (GRSP). It persists in soil for years.

manas.q: What is glomalin?

children.note: Hyphae physically bind soil particles and glomalin helps glue them, giving crumbly soil that resists erosion and lets water in.
Glomalin and hyphae add to stable soil organic carbon, which is one reason AMF matter in regenerative farming.
Benefits beyond nutrition, which vary with crop and conditions.
Mycorrhizal plants often cope better with dry spells because hyphae keep supplying water and nutrients from a larger soil volume.

manas.q: How do mycorrhizae help plants cope with drought?

children.note: Colonised roots can show less damage from some root rots and nematodes, partly through competition and stronger plant defences. Protection is partial, not a fungicide substitute.
Pre-colonised seedlings usually establish faster after transplanting.
Most crops form AM. A few families do not.
Maize, sorghum, millets, beans, cowpea, soybean, onion, leek, cassava, sweet potato, tomato, pepper, citrus, coffee, tea, banana and most fruit trees.
Crops with coarse roots and few root hairs, like onion, leek, citrus, cassava and many tree crops, depend most on mycorrhiza.

manas.q: Which kinds of crops depend most on mycorrhiza?

children.note: The cabbage family (cabbage, kale, mustard, canola) and the beet family (beet, spinach, amaranths) generally do not form AM. Lupins are also poor hosts.

manas.q: Which crop families do not form arbuscular mycorrhiza?

children.note: Low-P soils, eroded or newly levelled land, sterilised or soilless nursery media, and fields after long fallow or after non-host crops.
Stunted plants with dark green or purplish older leaves (phosphorus shortage) despite adequate P in the soil test may signal poor root uptake.
Colonisation cannot be seen by eye. Labs stain cleared roots and count infected root length under a microscope.
Because AMF need a host, inoculum is grown on host plant roots. No brand names here.
A mix of spores, colonised root pieces and hyphae in a carrier such as vermiculite, sand or clay granules.
Labels state viable propagules or spores per gram. Propagules include spores, hyphae and root bits that can start colonisation. Compare products by this count.

manas.q: What does 'propagules per gram' measure on a mycorrhiza label?

children.note: Finer spore powders suit seed coating and drip; granules suit furrow placement.
TNAU grows inoculum in polythene-lined trenches of vermiculite and soil with maize as the host, harvesting after about 60 days.
Keep cool and dry, out of sun. Spores are tougher than bacteria, but heat and moisture still reduce viability.
The fungus must touch roots. Place it in the root zone, not on the surface.
TNAU suggests about 100 g of bulk inoculum per square metre mixed into the nursery bed before sowing.
Mix about 5–10 g of inoculum into each bag of potting mix, per TNAU guidance.
Place about 20 g per seedling in the planting hole, under and around the roots, per TNAU guidance.

manas.q: Where should mycorrhizal inoculum be placed at transplanting?

children.note: TNAU gives about 200 g per tree, placed into holes or trenches dug in the active root zone.
Place in the seed furrow or coat seed so spores sit beside young roots. Tea guidance from TNAU is about 4 kg per acre.
Works well with compost, Azospirillum, Azotobacter, Rhizobium and PSB. Keep chemical fungicides away from the root zone at application.
Many common practices reduce native and introduced mycorrhiza.
When soluble P is plentiful the plant stops feeding the fungus and colonisation drops. Use moderate P, ideally banded.

manas.q: Why does heavy P fertiliser reduce mycorrhiza?

children.note: Several soil-applied and systemic fungicides harm AMF. Avoid drenches and in-furrow fungicides where inoculum is used.
Ploughing tears the hyphal network and dilutes spores, so plants must rebuild colonisation each season.

manas.q: How does tillage harm mycorrhiza?

children.note: Without living roots AMF starve. After long fallow, crops can show P deficiency even in fertile soil ('long fallow disorder').

manas.q: What is long fallow disorder?

children.note: A season of brassicas or beet lowers spore numbers for the next crop.
Waterlogged paddies and soil fumigation or solarisation sharply reduce AMF.
Often the cheapest route is to protect the fungi already in your soil.
Grow cover crops or intercrops between main crops so AMF always have a host.
Minimum or zero tillage keeps networks intact.
Follow non-host crops with strong hosts like maize, sorghum or legumes to rebuild spores.
Results are real but vary widely. Mycorrhiza is not a fertiliser and adds no P of its own.
Responses are largest in P-poor soils, in sterilised nursery media and in highly dependent crops, and smallest in high-P soils.
In fields with healthy native AMF, added inoculum may give little extra benefit. Test with untreated strips on your own farm.
Mycorrhiza can let you use P more efficiently and sometimes reduce P rates, but crops still need adequate nutrients overall.
Common errors with mycorrhizal products.
Spores scattered on dry surface soil rarely reach roots. Always place inoculum in the root zone.
Inoculating cabbage, kale or beet wastes money because they are non-hosts.
Heavy soluble P at the same time cancels much of the benefit.
Once roots are colonised, extra inoculum adds little. Placement and quality matter more than quantity.
Local context for using mycorrhiza.
Mycorrhizal biofertilizers are covered by the Fertiliser (Control) Order, which sets quality standards that products must meet.
Check that products are registered with the relevant Kenyan regulators (KEPHIS; PCPB where pest or disease claims are made).
Fruit tree, tea, coffee and forestry nurseries in both countries are the most practical starting point for inoculation.

nodeData.note: Trichoderma is a group of soil fungi used as a biological fungicide. It attacks and crowds out root-rotting fungi and also helps roots grow, so it is mainly used to prevent soil-borne diseases rather than cure them.

children.note: A fast-growing, free-living soil fungus found in most soils, especially those rich in organic matter. Colonies turn green as they produce spores.
Trichoderma is a filamentous fungus (mould), not a bacterium. It lives freely in soil and on roots and decaying organic matter, not inside a host plant.

manas.q: Is Trichoderma a bacterium or a fungus?

children.note: One of the earliest and most widely used species in Indian biocontrol products, used for seed treatment and soil application against root rots and wilts.
A very common biocontrol species, valued for strong mycoparasitic activity against soil fungi such as Rhizoctonia and Sclerotium.
A species used in many newer registered products, including in Kenya; it colonises roots well and is used against root rots and wilts.
In culture or on enriched manure it first grows as white threads, then becomes dark green as it sporulates. The green colour is a quick field sign of good growth.

manas.q: What colour does a mature Trichoderma colony turn?

children.note: Trichoderma protects roots through several actions at once, which is why pathogens rarely become resistant to it.
Trichoderma coils around the threads of disease fungi and dissolves their walls with enzymes such as chitinases and glucanases, then feeds on them.

manas.q: What is mycoparasitism?

children.note: It grows quickly and occupies root surfaces and organic matter first, taking space and nutrients that pathogens need to infect the root.
It releases antifungal compounds, including volatile and non-volatile metabolites, that slow or stop the growth of nearby pathogens.
When it colonises roots, the plant's own defence system is primed, so the whole plant responds faster to later attacks.

manas.q: Besides attacking pathogens directly, how does Trichoderma protect the whole plant?

children.note: Many strains improve root branching and help nutrient uptake, partly by solubilising some nutrients and producing growth-promoting substances. Effects vary with strain and soil.
It works best against soil-borne fungal diseases and is preventive. It is not a remedy for leaf diseases or for crops already badly infected.
Seedlings rot at the soil line or fail to emerge in nurseries. Trichoderma in seed treatment and nursery media is a standard preventive measure.

manas.q: Which nursery disease is Trichoderma seed treatment mainly used to prevent?

children.note: Roots become brown or black and decay, causing poor growth and plant death; common in pulses, cotton, vegetables and many other crops.
Fungal wilts block the water-conducting tissue, so plants droop and die even when the soil is moist.
Main targets are soil fungi and fungus-like organisms that attack roots and stem bases.
Causes vascular wilts in tomato, banana, chickpea, pigeonpea and others. Trichoderma reduces infection pressure but cannot cure an already wilted plant.
Causes damping off, root rot and sheath blight; often seen as brown sunken lesions at the stem base.
A water mould (oomycete) favoured by waterlogged soil; a major cause of seedling damping off.

manas.q: Which damping-off pathogen is favoured by waterlogged soil?

children.note: Sclerotium rolfsii causes collar rot and southern blight; it forms white fan-like growth and mustard-seed-like sclerotia at the stem base.
Recognising soil-borne disease early helps decide when Trichoderma should be part of the plan.
Pre-emergence damping off shows as gaps in rows; post-emergence shows thin, water-soaked stems that topple over.

manas.q: What does post-emergence damping off look like?

children.note: Pulled-up plants show decayed, soft or dry rotted roots with few fine roots.
Splitting the lower stem of a Fusarium-wilted plant shows brown discoloured vessels; wilting often starts on one side.

manas.q: What do you see when you split the stem of a Fusarium-wilted plant?

children.note: White cottony growth with small round brown sclerotia at the stem base points to Sclerotium collar rot.
Fewer gaps in nursery beds, healthier white roots, less wilting over seasons; green Trichoderma growth may be visible on enriched manure.
Use it before disease appears: on seed, in the nursery, in manure and in the soil. Follow the label dose; values below are common extension recommendations.
Seed is coated with the powder, often about 4 g per kg seed with a little water or sticker, dried in shade and sown the same day.

manas.q: What is a common Trichoderma seed-treatment dose?

children.note: Mix the product into nursery soil or cocopeat and drench seedling trays to protect young seedlings from damping off.
Dip transplant roots in a Trichoderma suspension for a short time before planting to give them a protective coat.
Mix the product with well-decomposed, moist farmyard manure, cover with a wet sack in shade, turn occasionally and apply after about 1–2 weeks when green growth appears.

manas.q: How do farmers multiply Trichoderma on the farm before soil application?

children.note: Enriched FYM is broadcast in furrows or around plants at sowing or planting, and repeated in perennial crops at the root zone.
A water suspension is poured around the stem base of seedlings or established plants to protect the root zone.
It needs moist soil and organic matter to establish. Dry soil, direct sun on the product and very low organic matter reduce its survival.
Generic product types; check registration, CFU count and expiry date on every pack. No single form suits every farm.
The most common form in India: spores mixed with talc or another inert carrier. Easy for seed treatment and FYM enrichment.
Liquid and wettable-powder forms suit drip, drenching and spraying, and often have longer shelf life than plain talc products.
Strength is given in colony-forming units per gram. Indian registration guidelines for talc Trichoderma require at least about 2 × 10⁶ CFU per gram.

manas.q: What does CFU on a Trichoderma label mean?

children.note: Talc products typically keep about 6 months; keep in a cool, dry, shaded place and use before the expiry date.

manas.q: How should Trichoderma products be stored?

children.note: Some products combine Trichoderma with bacterial agents such as Pseudomonas; check that the label lists each organism and its count.
Living fungus: many chemical fungicides kill it, while organic manures help it.
Systemic fungicides such as carbendazim and other benzimidazoles are particularly harmful. Do not mix it in the same seed treatment or tank.

manas.q: Why should Trichoderma not be mixed with carbendazim?

children.note: If a chemical fungicide must be used, apply it separately and leave a gap before using Trichoderma, as advised by local extension.
Compost, FYM and neem cake give it food and help it build up in soil.
It is commonly used alongside Rhizobium, Azotobacter or PSB; apply on the same seed in sequence, with the biofungicide first, as advised.
Treat it as one part of integrated disease management, not a guarantee.
Best results come when it is applied before or at sowing. It cannot revive plants already wilted or rotted.
Repeated use with organic matter builds up suppressive soil; benefits are often clearer after several seasons.
Soil moisture, temperature, organic matter, strain and product quality all change how well it works.
Common errors that waste money or kill the product.
Using it in the same seed treatment as a chemical fungicide can kill the spores and leave seed unprotected.
Without moisture and organic matter it struggles to establish; always apply to moist soil, ideally with manure.
It mainly protects against soil-borne fungi. Leaf spots, viruses and insect pests need other measures.
Spores die with age and heat; an old pack may contain few living units.
Biocontrol agents are regulated as biopesticides, not fertilizers.
Trichoderma products are registered as biopesticides under the Insecticides Act with the Central Insecticides Board; buy registered products.

children.note: In Kenya, Trichoderma products must be registered by the Pest Control Products Board; KEPHIS handles plant health and imported microbes.
Trichoderma is widely accepted in organic production; check certifier rules for the specific product.

nodeData.note: Three groups of beneficial bacteria used as biological disease control agents. They protect plants by producing antibiotics, competing for iron and space, and switching on the plant's own defences.

children.note: A common root-colonising bacterium used as a biocontrol and growth-promoting agent in many crops.
A free-living, rod-shaped, Gram-negative bacterium that lives on root surfaces (rhizobacterium). It glows yellow-green under UV light on certain media.

manas.q: Is Pseudomonas fluorescens a fungus or a bacterium?

children.note: It makes iron-binding molecules that grab scarce iron in the root zone, starving pathogens of iron.

manas.q: How do siderophores help suppress pathogens?

children.note: Strains produce antimicrobial compounds such as 2,4-diacetylphloroglucinol, phenazines and pyoluteorin that inhibit fungi and bacteria.
Root colonisation primes defences throughout the plant, so leaves can resist some diseases even though the bacteria stay at the roots.

manas.q: What is induced systemic resistance (ISR)?

children.note: It can improve root growth and nutrient uptake, partly through plant hormones and phosphate solubilisation in some strains.
Used against a range of fungal and some bacterial diseases, mostly as a preventive.
In India it is widely recommended for rice, used as seed treatment, seedling dip and foliar spray to reduce blast and sheath blight.
Can lower bacterial wilt in solanaceous crops when combined with resistant varieties, rotation and hygiene, but it is not a stand-alone cure.
Protects roots against Pythium, Rhizoctonia and Fusarium in nurseries and field crops.
As a non-spore-former it is more sensitive to heat and drying than Bacillus, so storage and shade matter more.
Spore-forming bacteria that make tough, long-lasting biocontrol products.
A Gram-positive, spore-forming soil bacterium used against many fungal leaf and root diseases.

manas.q: Why do Bacillus products usually have a longer shelf life?

children.note: A close relative of B. subtilis, known for strong antifungal lipopeptides and root colonisation.
Many strains formerly sold as B. amyloliquefaciens are now classified as B. velezensis; it is a strong producer of antimicrobial compounds.

manas.q: What is the newer name for many biocontrol strains once called B. amyloliquefaciens?

children.note: Bacillus forms resting spores that survive heat, drying and long storage, which gives products longer shelf life.
They produce compounds such as surfactin, iturin and fengycin that damage fungal cell membranes.

manas.q: Name the lipopeptide antibiotics made by Bacillus.

children.note: Used as seed treatment and drench for root diseases and as foliar spray against some leaf and fruit fungi; also induces plant resistance.
Filamentous soil bacteria (actinomycetes) and the source of many medical antibiotics.
Gram-positive bacteria that grow as branching threads like fungi and give soil its earthy smell (geosmin).

manas.q: What gives freshly dug soil its earthy smell?

children.note: Produces antifungal and antibacterial compounds, enzymes that break down fungal walls, and colonises roots to compete with pathogens.
Biocontrol species such as S. griseoviridis and S. lydicus are used against root rots and damping off, mainly in vegetables and nurseries.
Know the symptoms these agents are used to prevent.
Spindle-shaped spots with grey centres and brown margins on leaves; neck blast causes empty, broken panicles.

manas.q: What do rice blast leaf spots look like?

children.note: Oval greenish-grey lesions on sheaths near the waterline that enlarge and merge.
Whole plants wilt suddenly while still green; a cut stem in clear water releases milky bacterial streams.

manas.q: What simple test points to bacterial wilt?

children.note: Seedlings collapse at the soil line, and older plants have brown, decayed roots and stunted growth.
Common extension practices; always follow the label dose and timing.
Coat seed with the powder and a little water just before sowing; Pseudomonas is often used at about 10 g per kg seed.

manas.q: What is a common Pseudomonas seed-treatment dose?

children.note: Soak transplant roots, for example rice seedlings, in a suspension for about 30 minutes before planting.
Mix the product with well-decomposed FYM or compost and apply to moist soil at sowing or planting.
Liquid products can be poured around the stem base or given through drip for root-zone diseases.
Used for some leaf diseases such as rice blast; spray in the cool evening so UV and heat do less damage.
Generic forms; no brand names. Check registration number, CFU count and expiry.
Carrier-based powder common in India; easy for seed treatment and FYM enrichment, typically with about 6 months' shelf life.
Suited to drip, drench and spray; usually longer shelf life than powders when stored correctly.
Bacillus products are often sold as wettable powders or granules because their spores remain stable.
Strength is stated as CFU per gram or ml; the registration sets a minimum for each organism. Choose fresh packs with clearly stated counts.
Keep cool, dry and out of sunlight; never leave packs in a hot vehicle or store.
Living bacteria must be kept away from chemicals that kill them.
Copper fungicides and bactericidal antibiotics such as streptomycin can kill these bacteria; do not tank-mix.

manas.q: Which chemicals kill bacterial biocontrol agents in a tank mix?

children.note: Bacteria often tolerate some fungicides better than Trichoderma does, but compatibility varies; check the label or separate applications.
Pseudomonas and Trichoderma are often used together or in consortium products to cover more pathogens.
FYM, compost and neem cake improve survival and spread in soil.
Where these agents are most often used.
Pseudomonas is a common part of rice disease management in India, from seed to transplanting and spray.
Seed treatment and tray drenches protect tomato, chilli, brinjal and cabbage seedlings from damping off.
Applied with FYM to the root zone to help against soil-borne wilts and rots, alongside clean planting material.
Seed treatment helps protect against root rot and wilt in early growth stages.
Use them as part of integrated disease management.
They reduce disease pressure when applied early; they do not cure plants that are already badly infected.
Strain, product quality, soil, weather and timing all affect how well they work in the field.
Common errors with bacterial biocontrol.
These agents work best preventively; spraying only after heavy infection gives poor results.

children.note: Effect depends strongly on the strain; two Bacillus products can perform very differently.
UV and heat kill Pseudomonas quickly; mix in shade and use the suspension the same day.
These products are regulated as biopesticides.

nodeData.note: Living fungi, bacteria, viruses and nematodes that make insect pests and nematodes sick. They act more slowly and more selectively than chemical pesticides and work best as part of integrated pest management (IPM).

children.note: Microbial biopesticides are products whose active ingredient is a living microorganism (or its toxin) that infects or poisons a pest.
Fungi (Beauveria, Metarhizium, Lecanicillium, Purpureocillium), bacteria (Bacillus thuringiensis), viruses (NPV) and insect-killing nematodes.

manas.q: What are the four main groups of microbial biopesticides?

children.note: They are safe for people, livestock and most natural enemies, leave little or no harmful residue, and help manage pests that have become resistant to chemicals.
They kill slowly (days, not hours), need the right humidity, temperature and timing, and are living products that die if stored or mixed badly.
Best results come when they are applied early, when pest numbers are still low, and repeated. They are weak as a last-minute rescue in a heavy outbreak.

manas.q: Are microbial biopesticides best as early prevention or emergency rescue?

children.note: An insect-killing fungus found naturally in soils worldwide. It causes white muscardine disease in a wide range of insects.
A soil fungus (entomopathogen) that does not need to be eaten: its spores infect insects by touching their skin.

manas.q: Does Beauveria need to be eaten by the insect to infect it?

children.note: Spores stick to the insect cuticle, germinate and push through it with enzymes and pressure. The fungus grows inside the body, uses up its contents and releases toxins; the insect dies in several days.
Caterpillars, beetles and weevils (including banana weevil and coffee berry borer), stem borers, whiteflies, thrips, aphids and termites.
Dead insects become stiff and mummified, then are covered by a white, powdery or cottony fungal coat, first at the joints. This is proof the fungus is working.

manas.q: What colour is the fungal growth on insects killed by Beauveria?

children.note: Background on the fungus, its host range and its use in biological control.
An insect-killing soil fungus that causes green muscardine disease. It is especially useful against soil-dwelling pests.
A soil fungus that infects insects through the skin, like Beauveria. Related species (e.g. Metarhizium acridum) are used against locusts and grasshoppers.
White grubs, termites, root weevils, rhinoceros beetle in coconut, sugarcane and soil pests, plus locusts and grasshoppers (special strains).
Killed insects harden and get a white growth that turns olive to dark green as the fungus produces spores.

manas.q: What colour do insects killed by Metarhizium turn?

children.note: Mix the product with well-decomposed compost or FYM and place it in the root zone or planting hole, then keep the soil moist, so the fungus establishes where grubs live.
Background on Metarhizium species and their biology.
A fungus best known for attacking sap-sucking insects. Older literature calls it Verticillium lecanii.
An entomopathogenic fungus now named Lecanicillium (several species); the old name Verticillium lecanii is still printed on many labels.

manas.q: What is the older name of Lecanicillium lecanii?

children.note: Soft-bodied sucking pests: whiteflies, aphids, mealybugs, scales and thrips, mostly in greenhouses and humid crops.
Infected insects are covered with a white to cream fuzzy growth; scales and whitefly nymphs get a white halo around them.
It needs long periods of high humidity, so it suits greenhouses, dense canopies and rainy seasons better than dry open fields.
Taxonomy and biocontrol use of Lecanicillium.
A soil fungus (formerly Paecilomyces lilacinus) used against plant-parasitic nematodes, especially root-knot nematodes.
A common soil fungus that parasitises nematode eggs and females. Its old name, Paecilomyces lilacinus, is still widely used.

manas.q: Which pest group does Purpureocillium (Paecilomyces) lilacinus control?

children.note: Fungal threads grow into nematode egg masses and eggs, killing the developing juveniles, which lowers the next generation in the soil.
Roots with knots or galls, stunted, wilting plants in patches despite water, and yellowing: signs of root-knot nematode in tomato, vegetables, banana and pulses.
Mix with compost or neem cake, apply to nursery beds, planting holes or the root zone, or use as a seedling root dip; keep soil moist and repeat in later seasons.
Taxonomy and nematode-control use of the fungus.
A soil bacterium whose protein crystals poison caterpillars and some other insect larvae once eaten.
A spore-forming bacterium. When it forms spores it also makes crystal (Cry) proteins that are toxic to specific insect groups.
The larva must eat it. The gut's alkaline juice dissolves the crystal, the activated toxin punches holes in the gut wall, and the insect stops feeding within hours and dies in a few days.

manas.q: Why must Bt be eaten to work?

children.note: Subspecies kurstaki and aizawai target caterpillars (moths); israelensis targets mosquito and blackfly larvae; tenebrionis targets some beetle larvae.

manas.q: Which Bt subspecies is used against mosquito larvae?

children.note: Larvae stop feeding, become sluggish, darken and shrivel; damage stops quickly even though dead larvae may appear only after 2–3 days.
Spray young larvae, cover the leaves they feed on, and spray in the evening because sunlight (UV) breaks down the toxin.
Biology, toxins and uses of Bt.
Nuclear polyhedrosis viruses (baculoviruses) that infect caterpillars of one or a few closely related species.
A baculovirus packed in protein crystals (occlusion bodies). Each NPV is very host-specific, e.g. HaNPV for Helicoverpa armigera and SlNPV for Spodoptera litura.

manas.q: Why is each NPV product used only against one pest species?

children.note: Larvae eat virus on leaves; the crystals dissolve in the gut and the virus multiplies in body cells until the larva dies in about a week.
Infected larvae become pale and limp, climb to the top of the plant, hang head-down and burst, releasing fluid full of virus.

manas.q: How do NPV-killed caterpillars look and where are they found?

children.note: Spray in the evening on young larvae, add a sticker and keep sprays fresh. Farmers can collect virus-killed larvae, but quality is hard to control.
The virus family to which NPVs belong.
Microscopic roundworms (Steinernema, Heterorhabditis) that hunt and kill insects in soil with the help of bacteria they carry.
Beneficial nematodes in the genera Steinernema and Heterorhabditis. Only the infective juvenile stage lives free in soil, searching for hosts.
Juveniles enter the insect through mouth, anus or breathing holes and release symbiotic bacteria (Xenorhabdus or Photorhabdus) that kill it within 1–2 days.

manas.q: Which bacteria do insect-killing nematodes carry?

children.note: Soil and hidden pests: white grubs, cutworms, root weevils, fungus gnats and borers in tunnels.
Killed insects are soft, not mummified. Heterorhabditis kills turn brick-red; Steinernema kills turn brown to tan.

manas.q: What colour are grubs killed by Heterorhabditis?

children.note: Keep cool, use quickly, apply to moist soil in the evening, and water before and after so juveniles can move. Do not leave the mix in hot sun.
Biology of entomopathogenic nematodes.
Most failures come from timing, weather and handling, not from the organism itself.
Fungal spores need high humidity and leaf moisture for several hours to germinate. Spray when nights are humid, in rainy seasons, or under dense canopy.

manas.q: Why are fungal biopesticides weak in hot, dry weather?

children.note: Spray late afternoon or evening: sunlight UV kills spores and Bt and viruses, and night humidity helps fungi germinate.

manas.q: What is the best time of day to spray microbial biopesticides?

children.note: Cover the undersides of leaves and the parts where pests feed. Use clean water, a sticker or spreader if the label allows, and fine droplets.
Plan 2–3 sprays a week or so apart, or as on the label, because the products persist only a short time on leaves.
For soil pests, mix the product with moist, well-decomposed compost or FYM, incubate in shade for a few days if advised, then apply to the root zone.
Avoid chlorinated or very hard or alkaline water; let tap water stand, and use the spray mix within a few hours.
Living products can be killed by many farm chemicals, so check before mixing.
Chemical fungicides can kill Beauveria, Metarhizium and other fungal products. Keep a gap of several days and never tank-mix unless the label says so.

manas.q: Can you tank-mix Beauveria with a chemical fungicide?

children.note: Bt and NPV generally tolerate more chemicals, but strong alkaline or copper mixes can damage them; follow the label.
Neem products, compost, Trichoderma and other biologicals are often used in the same programme; check the label or a jar test first.
These products spare most predators and parasitoids, so they fit well with IPM and with conserving beneficial insects.
Mix small amounts in a jar in the same ratio; separation, clumping or heat means do not mix.
Shelf life depends on keeping the organism alive.
Store in a cool, dark, dry place, away from sun and chemicals. Nematode and some liquid products need refrigeration.
A good label states the organism and strain, spore or CFU count, manufacture and expiry dates, and registration number.
Old products have fewer live spores and give poor control even if the pack looks fine.
Common reasons farmers say biopesticides do not work.
Pests die in days, but feeding usually drops earlier. Judge the result after about a week, not the next morning.
Hot sun and dry air kill spores before they infect. Evening spraying is cheap insurance.
Large outbreaks or large larvae are hard to stop; scout early and start at low pest numbers.
Each organism has a host range; Bt does not kill aphids and NPV attacks only its own host species.
Biopesticides are regulated like other pest control products.
In Kenya, biopesticides must be registered by the Pest Control Products Board (PCPB) before sale or use; look for a PCPB number on the label.

manas.q: Which body registers biopesticides in Kenya?

children.note: Importing live microbes or natural enemies also involves KEPHIS plant-health rules, so new strains need extra approvals.
In India, biopesticides are registered by the Central Insecticides Board & Registration Committee under the Insecticides Act, not under the Fertiliser Control Order.

manas.q: Under which law are biopesticides registered in India?

children.note: Short videos on this topic from universities, extension services and experienced growers. Opens YouTube.

How the white muscardine fungus infects pests.
Mass producing and using Metarhizium.

nodeData.note: Compost is organic waste turned by microbes (and worms) into a stable, humus-rich material that feeds soil life. Making it well means managing food, air, water and temperature for the decomposers.

children.note: Compost improves soil structure, water holding and biological activity, and slowly releases nutrients.
Compost adds organic matter and a large, diverse population of microbes, which drive nutrient cycling and help suppress some soil-borne diseases.
Compost contains N, P, K and micronutrients but at low concentrations; it complements rather than fully replaces fertiliser for high-yield crops.

manas.q: Does compost fully replace fertiliser for high-yield crops?

children.note: Crop residues, manure and kitchen waste become a resource instead of a burning or disposal problem.
Fast aerobic composting in a heap that heats up, killing many weed seeds and pathogens.
Mix carbon-rich 'browns' (dry straw, leaves, stalks, sawdust) with nitrogen-rich 'greens' (fresh manure, green leaves, kitchen waste).
Microbes work fastest when the starting mix has roughly 25–30 parts carbon to 1 part nitrogen; too much carbon is slow, too much nitrogen smells of ammonia.

manas.q: What starting C:N ratio suits hot composting?

children.note: Keep the heap about 50–60% moisture: a squeezed handful should feel like a wrung-out sponge and release only a drop or two of water.

manas.q: How can you test compost moisture by hand?

children.note: Decomposers need oxygen. Turning the heap mixes it, lets in air and moves the outer material into the hot centre.
A good heap reaches about 55–65 °C in the core within days; holding this for several days kills many pathogens and weed seeds.

manas.q: What core temperature should a hot compost heap reach?

children.note: A warm mesophilic start, a hot thermophilic phase, a cooling phase, then maturation (curing) when fungi, insects and worms finish the job.
Build a heap large enough to hold heat (around 1 m wide and high is common), on well-drained ground, in shade and protected from heavy rain.
Push a metal rod into the core for a few minutes: too hot to hold means the heap is working; cold means it needs water, nitrogen or turning.
Compost made by surface-feeding earthworms eating pre-decomposed organic waste.
Worm castings plus partly digested material. It is fine, dark, granular and rich in microbes and plant-available nutrients.
The red wiggler or tiger worm: a surface-dwelling (epigeic) composting worm, tolerant of a range of conditions and widely used.

manas.q: What is the common name of Eisenia fetida?

children.note: The African nightcrawler: a large, fast-growing epigeic worm suited to warm tropical climates, but less tolerant of cold.

manas.q: Which composting worm suits warm tropical climates and is called the African nightcrawler?

children.note: Deep-burrowing field earthworms do not thrive in compost beds; use true composting (epigeic) species.

manas.q: Why can't any garden earthworm be used for vermicomposting?

children.note: Use a shaded pit, tank or bed with drainage, a base layer of coarse material, then partly decomposed waste and dung, covered with sacks or straw.
Pre-compost fresh material for a couple of weeks first; fresh heating waste, oily food, meat, onions and citrus in bulk harm worms.
Keep the bed moist but not waterlogged and cool; protect from sun, ants, rats and birds.
When the top is dark and granular, stop watering the top layer or heap it in light so worms move down or to fresh feed, then collect and sieve.
Background on vermicomposting methods and worms.
A liquid collected by passing water slowly through an active worm bed.
A brown liquid containing worm secretions, soluble nutrients and microbes washed from the bed and castings.

manas.q: How is vermiwash made?

children.note: A drum or tank with drainage layers, soil and worm-fed waste; water drips in from above and the leachate is collected at a tap at the bottom.
Dilute well with water and use as a foliar spray or soil drench; test on a few plants first, as strong solutions may scorch leaves.
Inoculants of fungi and bacteria added to speed composting of tough residues.
Mixed cultures of cellulose- and lignin-degrading fungi (e.g. Trichoderma, Aspergillus) and bacteria that break down straw, husk and stalks faster.
Tough coir pith is commonly composted with the oyster mushroom fungus Pleurotus plus a little nitrogen source, a well-known TNAU method.

manas.q: Which fungus is used to compost coir pith?

children.note: India's National Centre of Organic Farming released a waste decomposer culture that farmers multiply in jaggery water and spray on residues and heaps.
Inoculants cannot fix a heap that is too dry, too wet or too carbon-rich; moisture, air and C:N matter more.
A mixed liquid culture of beneficial microbes developed in Japan, used for composting, bokashi and soil.
EM was developed by Professor Teruo Higa in Okinawa, Japan, in the early 1980s.

manas.q: Who developed Effective Microorganisms (EM)?

children.note: Lactic acid bacteria (LAB), yeasts and phototrophic (purple non-sulfur) bacteria, grown together in a sugar-rich acidic liquid.

manas.q: What are the three main microbe groups in EM?

children.note: Produce lactic acid, lowering pH and suppressing rot organisms, which allows fermentation instead of putrefaction.
Use sugars and produce substances that feed the other microbes; they give EM its slightly alcoholic, sweet smell.
Use light and organic compounds for energy and help break down smelly sulphur compounds.
Stock EM is multiplied with molasses and clean water in a sealed container for about a week; good batches smell sweet-sour and turn acidic.
Many users report benefits, but scientific trials of EM give mixed results; treat it as one tool, not a cure-all.
An anaerobic fermentation of food waste using bran inoculated with EM or lactic acid bacteria.
Layers of waste and bokashi bran are pressed down in an airtight bucket; microbes ferment (pickle) the waste rather than rot it.

manas.q: Is bokashi aerobic composting or anaerobic fermentation?

children.note: Fill and seal for about two weeks, draining liquid from the bottom tap; the pickled waste then goes into a soil trench or compost heap to finish.
Fermented bokashi is acidic and raw; bury it away from roots and wait a few weeks before planting into it.
Background on the bokashi method.
Your nose, eyes and hand tell you how a heap is doing.
Dark brown, crumbly, with an earthy forest-floor smell; original materials not recognisable; cool after turning.

manas.q: How does mature compost look and smell?

children.note: Too many greens (nitrogen); add dry browns and turn.
Too wet and short of air; turn, add dry coarse material and improve drainage.

manas.q: What does a rotten-egg smell from a compost heap mean?

children.note: Too dry, too much carbon, or too small; add water and greens, make the heap bigger.
Exposed food or manure; cover with a layer of browns or soil and keep the heap closed.
Immature compost can harm crops by locking up nitrogen or releasing toxic compounds.
Unfinished compost keeps decomposing in the soil, can rob nitrogen from crops and may damage seedlings.
Sow cress or other quick seeds in moist compost next to plain soil; poor germination or yellowing means it is not ready.

manas.q: What simple test shows if compost is mature?

children.note: After turning and wetting, mature compost stays cool; if it heats up again, decomposition is still active.
India's Fertiliser (Control) Order sets standards for compost and vermicompost sold commercially; in Kenya, check national standards and registration rules before selling.
Sieve, store in shade under cover and keep slightly moist so microbes survive; do not let it dry to dust.
Compost is an ideal base to multiply and carry biofertilizers and biocontrol agents.
Compost provides food, moisture and shelter so introduced microbes such as Azotobacter, PSB or Trichoderma survive and multiply.
Add microbes only to cooled, mature compost; heat in an active heap kills them.

manas.q: Why should biofertilizers be added only to cooled compost?

children.note: Mix the biofertilizer with moist compost or FYM, keep in shade covered with a wet sack for several days, then apply to furrows or the root zone.
Do not mix the enriched compost with fresh chemical fertiliser or fungicide at the same time; keep them separate.
Common errors that slow composting or harm crops.
Fresh manure can burn roots, carry pathogens and weed seeds; compost it first.
Very heavy compost rates can add excess salts or phosphorus; apply according to soil and crop needs.
Hot composting kills many pathogens, but cold heaps do not; keep badly diseased material out of cold heaps.

nodeData.note: Liquids and solids that farmers ferment on the farm from dung, urine, plants, fish or forest soil to feed soil life and protect crops. They are cheap and local, but much of their reputation rests on field experience rather than controlled trials.

children.note: Why farmers make these inputs, how strong the evidence is, and the safety rules that apply to all of them.

They use free or cheap farm materials, cut cash spending, and add live microbes plus small amounts of nutrients and growth-active compounds. Many farmers also value the independence from bought inputs.

Most of these brews are dilute: they carry far less N, P and K than a crop removes. Their likely value is in stimulating soil biology and acting as biostimulants, so they work best on top of compost, manure and mulch.

manas.q: Are farm-made brews like Jeevamrut a major source of N, P and K?

children.note: Some claims are backed by controlled trials (neem extracts, vermiwash, fish hydrolysates), some by small or mixed trials (Panchagavya, Jeevamrut), and some mainly by farmer reports (IMO, FPJ, Dashaparni). This map labels which is which.
Dung and urine brews can carry gut bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella. Wear gloves, keep brews away from drinking water, and avoid spraying leafy vegetables or fruit eaten raw close to harvest.

manas.q: What is the main food-safety risk of dung-based brews?

children.note: Making an input for your own farm is generally unregulated, but selling it with claims is not. In India, biofertilisers and organic manures fall under the Fertiliser Control Order; in Kenya, pest-control products must be registered with the PCPB.
A fermented liquid of dung, urine, jaggery, pulse flour and a little soil, made as a cheap microbial booster. It is the core input of Subhash Palekar's Zero Budget Natural Farming (ZBNF).
A liquid microbial culture, not a fertiliser. It is meant to multiply soil microbes and stir earthworm activity in the root zone.

manas.q: Jeevamrut is the core input of which farming system?

children.note: Fresh cow dung and cow urine as the microbe source, jaggery as sugar food, pulse (gram) flour as protein, a handful of undisturbed soil from the farm as a local inoculum, and clean water.
Ingredients are mixed in a drum kept in the shade, covered loosely and stirred clockwise a few times a day. It ferments for a few days and is used soon after, while microbial activity is high.
Applied with irrigation water, poured near plant bases, or filtered and sprayed diluted on leaves. Farmers apply it repeatedly through the season, usually alongside mulch.

Studies find high microbial counts in fresh Jeevamrut and some gains in soil microbial activity. Yield results are mixed, and its nutrient content is very low, so it cannot by itself replace manure or fertiliser on poor soils.

India's National Academy of Agricultural Sciences questioned ZBNF claims in 2019 and asked for long-term trials. Andhra Pradesh scaled up a community-managed version of natural farming, which researchers are still evaluating.

manas.q: Which Indian academy questioned ZBNF claims in 2019?

children.note: The solid, dry form of Jeevamrut, made so the microbial mix can be stored and spread at sowing.
Dung mixed with the same additions as Jeevamrut, then heaped, shade-dried and crumbled into a coarse powder.

manas.q: How does Ghanjeevamrut differ from Jeevamrut?

children.note: Broadcast or placed in furrows or planting holes at sowing, often mixed into compost. Farmers report it keeps for some months if kept dry and shaded.
Very little controlled research exists. Its effect is probably similar to applying well-made compost or manure with some extra microbial inoculum.
A seed-treatment brew of dung, urine, lime and soil, used to coat seeds and seedlings before planting.
Cow dung and urine, a little lime (calcium hydroxide), a handful of farm soil, and water, soaked overnight.
Seeds are coated or soaked briefly, then dried in the shade before sowing. Seedling roots can be dipped before transplanting.

manas.q: What is Beejamrut used for?

children.note: A few small studies report better germination or seedling vigour, but evidence against seed-borne disease is limited. Proven biofertiliser seed treatments such as Rhizobium or Trichoderma have stronger data.
If also using a bought biofertiliser on the seed, do not mix it with lime-based brews; the high pH and salts can harm the inoculant. Treat separately and sow soon after.
A fermented mix of five cow products, used mainly as a diluted foliar growth promoter. It was popularised in Tamil Nadu and has been studied there by TNAU researchers.
Panchagavya means five products of the cow: dung, urine, milk, curd and ghee. Many recipes add jaggery, ripe banana and tender coconut water.

manas.q: What are the five cow products in Panchagavya?

children.note: Ingredients are added in stages and fermented in an open-mouthed container in the shade for a few weeks, with daily stirring, until it smells sweet-sour.
Filtered and sprayed on leaves well diluted, sometimes used for seed soaking or applied with irrigation. Typical timing is at key growth stages such as before flowering.
Analyses find lactic acid bacteria, yeasts and some growth-active compounds. A number of Indian field trials report better growth or yield, but trial quality varies and the mechanism is unclear.
Milk, curd and ghee make it costlier than other brews. Strong mixtures can scorch leaves, so test dilution on a few plants first.
Plant-based pest sprays, from neem extracts to the ten-leaf Dashaparni brew. This is the best-researched group in this map, mainly because of neem.

Leaves of about ten bitter or aromatic plants, often including neem, karanj, custard apple, castor and papaya, are soaked in cow urine and dung for several weeks. The filtered liquid is sprayed as a pest repellent.

manas.q: What does 'Dashaparni' refer to?

children.note: Neem seed kernels contain azadirachtin, which deters feeding, disrupts insect moulting and reduces egg laying. It acts slowly and mainly on young larvae and sucking pests rather than killing on contact.

manas.q: Which compound in neem gives most of its pest-control effect?

children.note: Crushed neem kernels soaked in water and filtered give NSKE, a well-studied home-made spray. Leaf extracts are much weaker than kernel extracts.
Pungent extracts such as chilli, garlic and ginger mainly repel insects. Evidence is mostly from field use and small trials.
Spray in the evening, cover undersides of leaves, and repeat at short intervals because botanicals break down in sunlight. Start early, when pest numbers are low.
Natural does not mean harmless: some plants used, such as datura or tobacco, are toxic to people and livestock. Botanicals also affect some beneficial insects, so spray only when needed.
Neem grows widely along the coast and in dry areas, and Kenya is a historic pyrethrum producer. Commercial botanical products in Kenya need PCPB registration.
A liquid made by fermenting fish waste with sugar, used as a nitrogen-rich foliar and soil feed in Korean Natural Farming.
Fish heads, guts and bones are layered with an equal weight of jaggery or brown sugar in a closed jar and left for weeks until the fish dissolves into a dark liquid.

manas.q: What two main ingredients make fish amino acid?

children.note: Strongly diluted and sprayed or watered in during vegetative growth, when the crop needs nitrogen. Too strong a mix can burn leaves.
Fish protein hydrolysates are recognised biostimulants and supply amino acids and nitrogen; trials on commercial fish products are generally positive. Farm-made FAA varies a lot in strength.
Strong smell attracts flies and dogs, so seal and site the jar carefully. Filter well to avoid blocking sprayers and drip lines.
Indigenous microorganisms (IMO) are collected from local forest litter and multiplied step by step. The method was developed in Korea by Cho Han-kyu.
Cooked rice is placed in a wooden box under forest leaf litter and covered. After a few days it grows white mould, which is the starter culture.

manas.q: In KNF, what is used to capture IMO-1?

children.note: The mouldy rice is mixed with brown sugar to feed and stabilise the culture.
IMO-2 is diluted and mixed into rice bran or similar meal, kept moist under cover in a heap, and turned until white mycelium spreads.
IMO-3 is mixed with field soil so the microbes adjust to local conditions before being spread on beds or added to compost.

manas.q: What is added at the IMO-4 stage?

children.note: Peer-reviewed field research on IMO is scarce; most evidence is from practitioners. The process can also multiply unwanted moulds, so smell and colour checks matter.
A KNF extract made from fast-growing plant tips fermented with brown sugar, used as a growth tonic.
Young shoots, often collected before sunrise, are chopped and mixed with an equal weight of brown sugar. After about a week the liquid is drained off.

manas.q: What plant material is used to make FPJ?

children.note: Highly diluted as a foliar spray or in irrigation, often combined with other KNF inputs.
Little controlled research exists. Benefits are mainly farmer-reported, and the high sugar content can encourage mould on leaves if overused.
A KNF culture of lactic acid bacteria grown in rice-wash water and then milk.
Rice-wash water is left to sour for some days, then mixed with milk. Curds separate, and the clear yellowish serum underneath holds the bacteria.

manas.q: What liquid is used first to catch LAB in KNF?

children.note: Diluted for animal drinking water, sprayed in livestock houses to cut odour, added to compost, or used in crop sprays.
Lactic acid bacteria are well known in food and silage. Crop benefits from farm-made LAB serum are mainly field-reported, while odour reduction in livestock housing is the most consistent report.
The liquid that drains from an earthworm bed when water trickles through it.
A collection of soluble nutrients, worm secretions and microbes washed from vermicompost. It is different from compost tea, which is actively brewed.

manas.q: How is vermiwash collected?

children.note: Diluted with water and sprayed on leaves, or applied to soil. It is often combined with dilute cow urine as a foliar spray.
Indian studies report growth and yield gains in vegetables and some disease suppression. Nutrient content is low, so benefits are more as a biostimulant than as a fertiliser.
Practical rules that apply to all fermented inputs.
Microbial brews are most active within days of being ready. Store in shade, and discard brews that smell rotten rather than sour or earthy.
Strain through cloth to avoid blocked nozzles and drip emitters.

children.topic: Do not mix with chemical fungicides
children.note: Copper, sulphur and synthetic fungicides or bactericides kill the microbes in the brew. Keep a gap of several days between them.
Brews give their best results where soils already get compost, manure, mulch and living roots. On bare, poor soil they add little.
Treat one strip and leave a similar strip untreated, then compare growth and yield. This is the only way to know if a brew pays on your farm.

manas.q: What is the simplest way to know if a brew works on your farm?

children.note: Common overclaims and errors to avoid.
These brews supply very little nutrient. Removing fertiliser and manure on poor soils and relying only on brews usually lowers yields.
Strong doses can scorch leaves or create anaerobic, smelly soil. Follow dilution guidance and test first.
Claims that only local breeds' dung works are not backed by comparative studies. Dung from any healthy cattle carries diverse microbes.
Heat and direct sun kill microbes and speed up spoilage. Brew and store in shade.

nodeData.note: Farming that aims to rebuild soil health, water cycling and biodiversity while staying productive. It is defined more by principles and outcomes than by a fixed rulebook, and practices must fit the local context.

children.note: A family of practices that improve soil rather than mine it. It overlaps strongly with conservation agriculture, agroecology and organic farming.
There is no legal standard for 'regenerative'. Most definitions combine soil-health principles with goals for carbon, water, biodiversity and farm income.

manas.q: Is there one legal definition of regenerative agriculture?

children.note: Rather than banning inputs, many regenerative approaches judge success by measured change: soil carbon, infiltration, biology, yields and profit.
Organic farming is a certified standard that limits synthetic inputs. Regenerative farms may or may not use some synthetic inputs; their focus is soil function.
Six commonly taught soil-health principles. The first four come from soil-health extension work; integrating animals and respecting context are added by many regenerative farmers.
Limit tillage and heavy chemical shocks. Ploughing breaks soil aggregates and fungal networks and speeds the loss of organic matter.

manas.q: Why does ploughing reduce soil organic matter?

children.note: Mulch, residues or living plants protect soil from raindrop impact, heat and erosion and feed soil organisms.
Living roots release sugars that feed microbes for as many months of the year as possible. Bare fallows starve the soil food web.
More crop and plant species above ground support more diverse soil life and break pest and disease cycles.
Grazing, manure and crop–livestock links recycle nutrients and turn cover crops and residues into food and income.
What works depends on rainfall, soil, markets, land tenure and labour. Principles are universal; practices are local.

manas.q: Name the six regenerative soil-health principles.

children.note: Plants grown to protect and feed the soil rather than for sale. A green manure is a cover crop worked into or laid on the soil while green.
They protect soil, add organic matter, and legume covers fix nitrogen with Rhizobium. Deep roots open compacted layers and recycle leached nutrients.
A fast-growing tropical legume that produces a lot of biomass in a short time. It is a common green manure in India and is also grown in Africa.

manas.q: What is the botanical name of sunn hemp?

children.note: A legume that tolerates waterlogging and salinity, so it is popular as a green manure before rice in India. Some species also form stem nodules that fix nitrogen.

manas.q: Why is dhaincha suited to rice fields?

children.note: A vigorous climbing legume that smothers weeds and adds nitrogen and mulch. Its raw seeds contain L-dopa and must not be eaten or fed without proper processing.
A drought-tolerant legume that gives ground cover, fodder and edible beans, so it pays its way in East African mixed farms.
Slash, roll or incorporate the cover around flowering, when biomass is high and stems are still soft. Leaving it as surface mulch keeps the benefits of cover.
Covers use water and land that might grow a cash crop, seed can be scarce, and they need a plan for ending them. Start on a small area.
Covering the soil surface with plant material such as straw, stover, grass or prunings.
Mulch cuts evaporation, keeps soil cooler, suppresses weeds, stops splash erosion and feeds earthworms and termites as it decays.
Woody or straw mulches with a high carbon-to-nitrogen ratio can tie up nitrogen while they decompose. Keep them on the surface rather than mixing them in.

manas.q: Why can mixing straw into soil cause nitrogen deficiency?

children.note: In much of Africa, crop residues are also livestock feed and fuel. This competition is one of the biggest barriers to mulching in mixed farms.
In dry parts of Kenya, termites can remove surface mulch quickly. Coarser mulch and higher biomass help, and termites still improve infiltration.
Growing crops with little or no soil turning, opening only the planting line or hole.
Jab planters, rippers, direct seeders and hand-dug planting basins or zai pits let farmers plant without ploughing the whole field.
Better aggregate stability and infiltration, less erosion, lower fuel and labour for land preparation, and more timely planting.
Without tillage, weeds must be managed by mulch, covers, rotation, hand weeding or herbicides. Weed control is often the deciding factor in adoption.
A large global meta-analysis found no-till alone often lowers yields, but the gap shrinks when residue retention and rotation are added, and is smallest in dry climates.

manas.q: When does no-till perform best relative to ploughing?

children.note: Changing crops across seasons and growing more than one crop together.
Alternating cereals with legumes or other families breaks pest and disease cycles and lets legumes leave some nitrogen for the next crop.
Growing two or more crops in the same field at the same time, such as maize with beans, cowpea or pigeon pea, uses light, water and nutrients more fully.
LER compares an intercrop with sole crops. An LER above one means the mixture produces more on the same land than growing the crops separately.

manas.q: What does a land equivalent ratio above 1 mean?

children.note: Pigeon pea grows slowly at first and keeps growing after the companion crop is harvested, so it fits well with maize or groundnut in East and Southern Africa.
A habitat-management system for cereals developed by icipe in Kenya with Rothamsted Research. It controls stemborers and Striga using companion plants.
Desmodium planted between maize rows gives off smells that repel stemborer moths. It also fixes nitrogen and covers the soil.

manas.q: In push–pull, which plant does the 'push'?

children.note: Napier grass or Brachiaria around the plot attracts moths to lay eggs there. Many larvae fail to survive on Napier, and the grass is cut for fodder.
Desmodium root exudates trigger Striga seeds to germinate and stop them attaching to maize roots, so the weed seed bank declines over time.

manas.q: How does Desmodium suppress Striga?

children.note: A version using drought-tolerant greenleaf Desmodium and Brachiaria was developed for drier areas. Studies also report reduced fall armyworm damage.
Fewer pest losses, more soil nitrogen, and a steady supply of high-quality fodder that supports dairy cattle.
Desmodium seed can be scarce and costly, establishment takes time and labour, and farmers need training to manage it.
Growing trees with crops or livestock on the same land.
Trees provide shade, windbreaks, fodder, fuel, fruit and timber. Leguminous trees fix nitrogen and their leaf litter feeds the soil.
A thorn tree with reverse leaf phenology: it drops its leaves in the rainy season, so it does not shade crops and its leaf fall adds nutrients.

manas.q: What is unusual about Faidherbia albida's leaves?

children.note: Calliandra, Leucaena and Gliricidia give protein-rich fodder for dairy cows and goats and can be cut repeatedly.
FMNR protects and prunes stumps and wild seedlings that sprout naturally, restoring tree cover cheaply without nurseries.
Boundary trees like Grevillea are common in Kenyan highlands. World Agroforestry (now part of CIFOR-ICRAF) is headquartered in Nairobi.
Charcoal made by heating biomass with little oxygen (pyrolysis), added to soil as a long-lasting form of carbon.
Biochar is stable carbon that can last in soil for a very long time. Ash from open burning is not biochar.

manas.q: How is biochar made?

children.note: Benefits are strongest in acidic, highly weathered tropical soils, where biochar can raise pH and hold nutrients and water. On fertile soils gains are often small.
Fresh biochar can adsorb nutrients and briefly reduce availability. Soaking it in urine, compost or manure before use charges it with nutrients and microbes.
Kilns that smoke heavily harm health and the climate. Biochar made from contaminated waste can carry heavy metals.
Planned movement of livestock so pasture plants get time to recover between grazings.
Animals graze a paddock for a short time, then move on, leaving the grass to regrow its leaves and roots. Dung and urine are spread more evenly.
Damage comes from grazing plants again before they have recovered. Rest periods matter more than animal numbers alone.

manas.q: What causes overgrazing, according to grazing management principles?

children.note: Well-managed rotational grazing can improve pasture cover, but bold claims that it reverses desertification or offsets all livestock emissions are contested by many scientists.
Pastoral communities and conservancies use planned grazing and grass banks, but tenure, water points and drought shape what is possible.
FAO's conservation agriculture rests on three linked principles: minimal soil disturbance, permanent soil cover, and crop diversification.
Minimum soil disturbance, permanent organic soil cover, and diversified crops through rotation or intercropping. They work best together.

manas.q: What are FAO's three principles of conservation agriculture?

children.note: CA is promoted in semi-arid parts of Kenya such as Laikipia, Machakos and Embu, often with rippers, jab planters and planting basins.
Zai pits, tied ridges and planting basins catch rain where crops need it and pair well with CA in dry areas.
Residues needed for livestock, weed pressure, cost of herbicides and special planters, and short-term yield dips slow adoption.
How to tell whether practices are actually improving the soil.
SOC changes slowly, often over years. Sample the same spots, depth and season each time and use the same lab method to see real change.

manas.q: Why must SOC be sampled at the same depth and season each time?

children.note: Converting a carbon percentage into tonnes per hectare needs bulk density. Without it, claims of carbon gains are unreliable.
Push a ring or open-ended tin into the soil, pour in a set amount of water and time how long it takes to soak in. Faster infiltration usually means better structure.

manas.q: What does a simple infiltration ring test measure?

children.note: Drop dry soil clods into water: stable, well-aggregated soil holds together, while degraded soil collapses.
Count earthworms in a spadeful of soil and watch how quickly cotton strips or tea bags decompose. These give quick signs of soil life.
Track yields, input costs, labour and rainfall alongside soil tests. Soil gains only matter if the farm stays viable.
India's Soil Health Card scheme provides regular soil test reports. In Kenya, KALRO and private labs offer soil analysis.
Points where enthusiasm can outrun evidence.

children.topic: Not all carbon is new carbon
children.note: No-till can concentrate carbon near the surface without raising the total in the whole profile. Deep sampling is needed before claiming storage.
Some farms see yield dips in the first seasons while weeds, pests and nutrient cycling adjust.

children.topic: Carbon credits are not easy money
children.note: Measurement, verification and permanence rules are strict, and payments per small farm are often small.
